name: Nostra Money Market
label: Oracle Manipulation
rootCause:
Nostra Finance paused its Starknet money market on 2026-09-17 after a manipulated NSTR price feed let one account borrow roughly $3.5 million in ETH, STRK, USDC, USDT, WBTC, and DAI against inflated collateral. Public reporting indicates part of the proceeds was bridged to Ethereum, but primary transaction records and a full postmortem were not publicly available during this review.

Public reporting and Nostra’s initial disclosure indicate that the attacker manipulated the oracle price used to value NSTR collateral inside Nostra’s Starknet money market. The available evidence suggests the protocol accepted an inflated spot-derived NSTR valuation, allowing the attacker to over-borrow against collateral whose real market value was far lower. The exact oracle implementation, pool-selection logic, and vulnerable contract path were not publicly documented in the consulted primary materials.

name: Flamincome
label: Oracle Manipulation; Token & Share Accounting
rootCause:
On 2026-09-16, legacy Ethereum Flamincome vault contracts associated with Flamingo Finance were exploited through share-price manipulation. Public incident reports state that the attacker used an approximately $18 million USDT flash loan to inject value into a Convex-linked strategy accounting path, inflate VaultYUSDT valuation, and extract about $345,900 in profit.

Public reporting and third-party incident analyses attribute the exploit to unsafe asset accounting in a legacy Flamincome USDT strategy. The strategy reportedly counted a permissionlessly injectable Convex BaseRewardPool balance as protocol-owned assets, allowing an attacker to inflate VaultYUSDT share pricing through injected USDP/3CRV liquidity-provider tokens and redeem assets at an artificially favorable rate.

name: Startale
label: Access Control
rootCause:
On 2026-09-16, attackers exploited Startale ERC-7579 smart accounts on Ethereum by abusing an initialization flag that reportedly remained valid for an entire transaction. Public incident trackers state that the flaw allowed same-transaction re-initialization of newly deployed counterfactual accounts with attacker-controlled bootstrap logic, leading to the theft of about $2,876 from roughly 330 pre-funded accounts.

Publicly available incident descriptions attribute the exploit to improper initialization state handling in Startale ERC-7579 smart accounts on Ethereum. A transient-storage initialization flag used by initializeAccount reportedly persisted for the duration of the transaction, which allowed an attacker to re-initialize freshly deployed accounts within the same transaction and install a malicious bootstrap module. No official postmortem, verified vulnerable source code, or independently verified exploit transaction has been located in the available evidence.

name: Chainflip AMM
label: Bridge Logic Flaw
rootCause:
On 2026-09-12, Chainflip paused its cross-chain swap network after attackers exploited memo-handling logic in the protocol’s Tron USDT settlement path. Public incident disclosures state that malformed memos attached to validator-signed Tron transactions triggered duplicate refunds and drained 736,442.17 USDT across six unauthorized payouts.

Chainflip’s Tron integration accepted swap instructions from transaction memos on transfers that had already been signed by validators, including wrapped contract calls. Attackers attached new or malformed memos to validator-signed transactions, causing the witnessing and refund logic to interpret the same underlying transfer as a separate failed swap and issue duplicate payouts.

name: Dominion
label: Private Key Compromise
rootCause:
Dominion’s SILV treasury on Solana was compromised on 2026-09-11 after three of five multisig signers were exposed, letting the attacker move treasury SILV, sell into thin liquidity, and bridge proceeds across Chainflip. The key theft method is still unknown.

Three of five signers on Dominion’s Solana treasury and token-admin multisigs were compromised. That quorum let the attacker authorize treasury transfers, signer changes, and admin actions such as freezes and delegate movements. The chain does not show how the keys were stolen, and no vulnerable contract code has been identified.

name: ether.fi Liquid
label: Access Control; Arbitrary External Call
rootCause:
On 2026-09-11, an attacker exploited missing authentication in ether.fi Liquid's legacy Veda AtomicQueue contract on Ethereum. By supplying victim wallets with stale ERC-20 approvals as the solver parameter in solve(), the attacker drained about 14.45 liquidETH and 7.05 USDC, then swapped the assets into 15.45 ETH.

The legacy AtomicQueue contract accepted an arbitrary solver address in solve() without verifying that the caller was authorized to act for that solver. During settlement, the queue executed want.safeTransferFrom(solver, users[i], assetsToUser), allowing the attacker to spend tokens from wallets that had previously approved the queue contract.

name: Symbiosis
label: Bridge Exploit; Unbacked Cross-Chain Mint
rootCause:
On September 11, 2026, Symbiosis paused its native Bitcoin bridge after attackers exploited BridgeV2 flaws that allowed unbacked syBTC minting. An observed Ethereum liquidation converted part of the counterfeit supply into about 4.39 WBTC before the bridge was isolated.

Symbiosis later attributed the incident to two chained BridgeV2 logic flaws. The Bitcoin deposit decoder identified the sender from attacker-controlled transaction data, allowing the attacker to appear as both an approved depositor and bridge administrator. A second accounting flaw mishandled negative fees by subtracting a negative value, increasing the credited mint amount instead of reducing it. The combined bugs allowed a tiny confirmed BTC deposit to authorize massive unbacked syBTC issuance.

name: BeatXswap
label: Oracle Manipulation; Flash Loan
rootCause:
BeatXswap’s LV Convert contracts on BNB Chain were drained on 2026-09-09 after an attacker flash-borrowed BTX, pushed down the Pancake V3 spot price used as the only oracle, and minted LP against protocol-owned BTX. Public trackers put the loss at about 2.985 million BTX, roughly $77,512.

The converter contracts trusted a single Pancake V3 slot0() spot read for BTX pricing and reused that same manipulated quote to size the mint and the slippage floor. A same-transaction BTX dump could move the pool price before deposit() ran, so the contracts minted LP against a crashed oracle price and spent protocol-owned BTX reserves.

name: Zentra Finance
label: Logic Error
rootCause:
Zentra Finance's ctUSD reserve on Citrea was reportedly drained through a repayWithATokens accounting edge case that let debt clear without a matching aToken burn.

Reported cause: the custom aToken burn helper clamped an oversize burn to the caller's remaining balance instead of reverting, and the Pool burned variable debt before that helper ran in repayWithATokens().

name: WealthManagementV2
label: Private Key Compromise
rootCause:
WealthManagementV2 on BNB Chain lost 26,414 USDT on 2026-09-08 after a suspected owner-key compromise let an attacker rewrite plan parameters and mint inflated interest.

The reported cause was a suspected owner-key compromise combined with an unrestricted updatePlanConfig path. Once the attacker controlled ownership, the contract accepted a zero period and extreme multipliers, which inflated interest accounting and enabled withdrawal of 26,414 USDT.

name: Liquid Network
label: Bridge Exploit; Unbacked Cross-Chain Mint; Consensus Validation Bug
rootCause:
Liquid Network halted peg operations on 2026-09-06 after attackers reportedly exploited an Elements range-proof cache collision bug to mint unbacked L-BTC and redeem it for nearly 4,000 BTC from federation reserves. Public reporting states that about 3,400 BTC was later returned while roughly 598.5 BTC remained outstanding.

Public reporting attributes the incident to a consensus validation bug in the Elements codebase used by Liquid Network. Reported analyses state that range-proof verification cache keys were constructed from variable-length fields without explicit length prefixes, allowing cache-key collisions that caused nodes to reuse a cached successful verification result for different proof inputs. The resulting unbacked L-BTC was later redeemed through an otherwise valid peg-out flow.

name: Dream Health Chain
label: Protocol Logic; Reward Logic Flaw
rootCause:
Dream Health Chain lost about $71,800 on 2026-09-05 after an award state machine let a claimed reward be reset and paid again from a shared proxy balance on BNB Chain's BSC network.

The award workflow lacked per-award reserve locking and let participateAward() restore a claimed award to an unclaimed state, so claimAward() could pay the same fixed reward repeatedly from a shared proxy balance.

name: Reddio RedSonic Vault
label: Flash Loan; Token & Share Accounting
rootCause:
On 2026-09-05, Reddio’s RedSonic Vault on Ethereum lost about 9.25 ETH after permissionless stETH registration let the same raw stETH balance count toward two share classes and inflate rsvETH pricing in a flash-loan-driven single transaction.

The vault let anyone register a second ERC-20 share class while the ETH class priced itself from the vault’s raw stETH balance. That shared balance was counted in both classes, so depositing stETH through the newly registered class raised rsvETH NAV and enabled excess redemption.

name: Secured Finance Lending
label: Oracle Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Secured Finance’s Ethereum lending market was reportedly manipulated on 2026-09-05 through same-block order-book price inflation, with public trackers placing the loss at about $104,000.

Public reports indicate that the lending market valued collateral from the current block’s order-book average execution price, and self-trades were able to inflate that price enough to overstate collateral value before the borrow was executed. The exact on-chain transaction sequence and vulnerable historical contract revision were not established in the available public evidence.

name: Notional V1
label: Integer Overflow; Integer Truncation
rootCause:
Notional V1’s legacy Ethereum escrow lost about $1.73 million after an integer truncation in the free-collateral path let a 2^128 liability read as zero.

An unsafe signed-to-uint128 conversion in the V1 escrow’s ETH valuation path truncated an engineered 2^128 liability to zero, so the free-collateral check accepted an insolvent account and allowed withdrawals from the legacy escrow.

name: Ankr
label: Logic Error; Unbacked Mint
rootCause:
On 31 August 2026, a flaw in Ankr's ankrFLOW contract on Flow EVM allowed an attacker to mint 8.6 million unbacked ankrFLOW tokens and use them as collateral on More Markets, draining 15.5 million WFLOW (worth ~$410,000). Flow Foundation later replaced the reserve, ensuring no user deposits were lost.

The ankrFLOW Solidity contract did not enforce collateralization in its minting logic, enabling creation of unbacked tokens that broke the token's backing invariant.

name: Aquifer
label: Access Control; Arbitrary External Call
rootCause:
Aquifer, a Solana-based automated market maker, was exploited on 31 August 2026 for approximately $2.47 million. The incident involved attacker-controlled wallets on both Solana and Ethereum. There is a split in reporting between a contract access-control flaw (supported via chain forensic analysis) and a wallet compromise (supported by official and news coverage), with no published technical post-mortem confirming the root cause.

The precise cause is disputed. Chain forensics reconstruct a swap-path vulnerability in Aquifer's Solana program: failure to validate supplied token program and balance account, allowing an attacker to nominate a malicious program and forged balance to drain assets. However, Aquifer's official and major news statements describe the incident as a wallet/private-key compromise and explicitly state no contract bug was confirmed. There is no published source code or project-level post-mortem to resolve the mechanism.

name: Float Protocol
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Float Protocol was exploited on Ethereum mainnet on 31 August 2026. An attacker manipulated the Uniswap V3 pool's spot price to distort LP share values in Hypervisor contracts, enabling extraction of approximately 10.71 ETH (~$28,000). The attack relied on flash loans and lacked price validation safeguards.

Float Protocol Hypervisor contracts priced LP shares using immediate Uniswap V3 spot (slot0) price without TWAP or oracle validation. Large flash-loan-enabled swaps manipulated this spot price, resulting in inflated LP share calculations and repeated value extraction.

name: Balancer V1
label: Logic Error; Rounding Error
rootCause:
On August 30, 2026, an attacker exploited a rounding error in Balancer V1's join logic on Ethereum Mainnet, draining approximately $234,000 from five legacy pools by compressing WBTC reserves to near-zero and minting pool tokens for negligible input. The bug resulted from single-asset join math that incorrectly rounded in the user's favor when pool balances became very small.

Balancer V1's joinswapPoolAmountOut function allowed a user to specify pool-token output, and calculated the required token input using fixed-point math. When the pool's WBTC balance was reduced to near zero, the calculation rounded down, letting the attacker mint large amounts of BPT with a one-satoshi input. There was no effective minimum input or minimum balance enforcement in join paths.

name: Tectonic
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Tectonic on Cronos was hit by a TONIC price-manipulation exploit on 2026-08-30. Public reporting puts the affected value around $75 million, with about $6 million bridged to Ethereum before Cronos halted block production.

Tectonic accepted TONIC as collateral while the token’s spot price could be moved sharply because liquidity was thin. Once the manipulated price fed into borrowing power, the attacker could borrow liquid assets against inflated collateral. The exact incident-time oracle path and code revision were not independently verified here.

name: Fogo Foundation
label: Key Compromise; Compromised Privileged Wallet
rootCause:
On August 29, 2026, a wallet controlled by the Fogo Foundation was compromised, allowing an attacker to drain 400 million FOGO tokens,over 10% of circulating supply. The breach caused an 18% price crash and led to a mainnet halt. Forensic, technical, and on-chain specifics remain unreleased.

Reported compromise of a privileged Foundation-controlled wallet: the attack most likely exploited weaknesses in private key management or access control, but the specific method and operational setup have not been disclosed by the Fogo Foundation.

name: Full Sail
label: Oracle Manipulation; Oracle Misconfiguration
rootCause:
Full Sail, a DeFi DEX and vault protocol on Sui, confirmed user fund losses on August 29, 2026, after a suspected Switchboard oracle compromise. The exact loss amount and technical attack details remain unconfirmed.

Losses arose from Full Sail's reliance on compromised Switchboard oracle price feeds. The detailed vector,such as key compromise, implementation flaw, or misconfiguration,has not been published.

name: Permapod
label: Logic Error
rootCause:
Permapod experienced a security incident on ZIGChain on 29 August 2026. The incident's cause, mechanism, and impact remain unknown, with no confirmed loss or root-cause details available.

The root cause of the Permapod incident remains unknown due to the absence of technical, transaction, or post-mortem details in all available sources.

name: Ajna V2
label: Liquidation Logic Flaw
rootCause:
Ajna V2 suffered a reported $775,400 loss on Ethereum on 2026-08-28 after attackers exploited its liquidation accounting across multiple pools. One checked cbETH transaction shows 3.474032198249838476 WETH sent into the reported pool path and 48.127374524782420835 cbETH leaving before the 4 WETH funding leg was repaid.

Available evidence supports a flaw in Ajna V2's internal liquidation lifecycle. Public reconstructions place the exploitable sequence in the interaction of bucketTake, collateral removal, take, and settlement, allowing collateral to leave a pool without matching quote repayment. The exact defective line and the incident-time deployed revision were not independently verified from primary code evidence.

name: Avici
label: Authorization flaw; Withdrawal logic flaw
rootCause:
Avici’s Solana card contract was exploited on 2026-08-28, affecting 1,685 users and $500,859.22 in card balances. Public reports attribute the drain to an authorization flaw in an outdated Rain card contract that let the attacker register collateral-admin privileges and withdraw funds.

Reported authorization and withdrawal-logic flaw in an outdated Rain Solana card contract used by Avici. Public reconstructions say the attacker reused a signature path to add collateral-admin authority and then withdraw card balances from affected accounts.

name: Virtue
label: Oracle Signing Key Compromise; Price Manipulation
rootCause:
On August 28, 2026, Virtue protocol on IOTA suffered a critical oracle signing key compromise, enabling an attacker to manipulate price feeds and mint roughly 4.94 million VUSD against a single IOTA deposit. The manipulated price soon triggered 47 liquidations across 45 user positions, freezing the protocol and causing up to $905,000 in affected collateral, with Virtue estimating damage at $455,000 and DefiLlama listing $894,500.

Compromise of Switchboard oracle signing keys allowed attacker-controlled price reporting, bypassing Virtue's feed authentication and enabling artificial collateral valuation with no economic sanity or deviation checks.

name: CashCowCoin (CCC)
label: Protocol Logic; Swap Logic Flaw
rootCause:
CCC, also referred to as CashCowCoin in secondary coverage, was reported exploited on BNB Chain for about $117,000 after a sell() path burned liquidity-pair tokens and skewed the AMM reserve ratio. The full transaction trace and trigger path were not public in the available record.

A swap logic flaw in CCC's sell() path let the token contract alter the liquidity pair's CCC balance and then re-sync around the changed reserve state. The exact trigger path and access-control failure remain unknown from the available evidence.

name: Moonwell Lending
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Moonwell's MAMO lending market on Base was exploited on August 27, 2026, via a sequence combining direct collateral-accounting inflation and spot price oracle manipulation. The attacker used thin-liquidity MAMO markets to spike the token’s oracle price, inflated collateral value, and borrowed assets totaling approximately $11M, with a net loss at $8.7M,$9M. Emergency response capped borrowing and supply immediately.

Moonwell's Base deployment counted thin-liquidity MAMO as loan collateral, relying on an uncompounded spot oracle price without minimum liquidity, deviation bounds, or a TWAP. The attacker directly increased the mMAMO exchange rate by transferring MAMO into the contract, then manipulated the MAMO/USD feed, amplifying both the share value and the oracle input.

name: CometDEX
label: Logic Error; Incorrect Share Accounting
rootCause:
CometDEX suffered a $717K exploit on Stellar on 25 August 2026, when attackers drained pooled assets by repeatedly looping flash loans through a same-asset swap flaw in the AMM's share accounting logic.

Broken share accounting in the Blend AMM contract allowed repeated same-asset swaps (USDC→USDC), corrupting reserve values and enabling attackers to systematically extract funds using flash loan loops. The contract failed to enforce exchange invariants or restrict swaps to different assets.

name: Enjin
label: Storage-slot collision; Missing owner-approval check; Malicious adapter registration
rootCause:
On August 25, 2026, an attacker exploited a storage-layout mismatch and missing approval checks in Enjin's Ethereum-based Crypto Items platform, draining approximately 5.24 million ENJ (~$142,000,$162,000) from the platform reserve via a single Ethereum transaction. The attacker used a malicious transfer adapter to bypass standard authorization safeguards and melted stolen NFTs for their ENJ backing.

A vulnerable per-item transfer adapter lacked owner-approval verification due to a storage-slot collision and unprotected initialization. This allowed unauthorized transfers of ENJ-backed Crypto Items, leading to their melting and reserve fund drain.

name: FH Token
label: Sell logic flaw; Reserve/accounting manipulation
rootCause:
FH Token was exploited on BNB Chain on August 25, 2026, via a flaw in its sell-tax logic, allowing the attacker to drain about $20,000 from the PancakeSwap FH/USDT pool through repeated buy-sell loops that manipulated token reserve accounting.

A vulnerability in FH Token's _transfer function and isSell logic caused premature token burns and an incorrect sync, allowing manipulated reserve inflation and repeated pool draining.

name: Steakhouse Financial
label: Risk Parameter Abuse
rootCause:
Steakhouse Financial’s 2026-08-25 incident was reported as a $920,000 Ethereum loss tied to risk parameter abuse, but the accessible record does not identify the exact contract path, transaction hash, or recovered funds.

Risk parameter abuse is the reported failure mode, but the exact parameter, contract, and state transition are not identified in the accessible sources.

name: Nesa
label: Logic Error
rootCause:
Nesa Chain disclosed malicious activity on 2026-08-24 tied to a vulnerability in the shared Cosmos EVM module used by several Cosmos SDK networks. Public reporting stated that an attacker inflated NES balances on Nesa, bridged manipulated tokens to Ethereum, and attempted to liquidate them through decentralized exchanges, although realized proceeds were reportedly far smaller than the nominal inflated value.

Public reporting consistently attributed the incident to a balance-accounting vulnerability in the shared Cosmos EVM module used by Nesa and other Cosmos SDK chains. The exact vulnerable function, arithmetic failure mode, and patched code path were not publicly confirmed in the consulted evidence.

name: Arrakis V1
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Arrakis V1's ENS,WETH Uniswap V3 vault on Ethereum was exploited on 23 August 2026 via a spot price manipulation, allowing an attacker to profit 2.94 WETH (~$7,100) in a single flash-loan-enabled transaction by distorting vault share pricing.

The ArrakisVaultV1 contract's mint() and burn() functions valued deposits and withdrawals using the live Uniswap V3 slot0() spot price. No time-weighted average price (TWAP) or deviation checks protected these operations, enabling an attacker to move the pool price within one transaction and capture manipulated value.

name: TermFinance Vaults
label: Governance Attack; Malicious Proposal
rootCause:
On August 23, 2026, TermFinance Vaults on Ethereum was compromised in a governance exploit, resulting in the theft of approximately $8.5 million in WETH and USDC. The attacker used a malicious proposal to disable safety timelocks and drain the vaults through the system's own execution path.

The protocol's governance module allowed a malicious proposal from an attacker with a trivial stake to bypass review, disable the enforced execution timelock, and direct vault funds to a malicious contract. No effective veto or proposal threshold blocked this path, enabling withdrawal of nearly all assets by anyone able to queue such a proposal.

name: warp.green
label: Bridge Exploit; Bridge Logic Flaw
rootCause:
warp.green's ERC-20 cross-chain bridge was exploited on August 23, 2026, resulting in the loss of approximately $93,000 in USDC. The exploitation originated from a logic flaw in the Chia-side bridge module, affecting USDC movements between Chia, Ethereum, and Base. There is no confirmed technical postmortem, on-chain transaction hash, or address available.

A logic flaw in the Chia-side module of warp.green's ERC-20 bridge allowed an attacker to present worthless CAT tokens as burned wUSDC, bypassing validator checks and draining bridge funds.

name: KiiChain
label: Logic Error; Arithmetic Underflow
rootCause:
On 2026-08-22, KiiChain halted block production after an attacker exploited chained balance-accounting flaws in the shared Cosmos EVM module. KiiChain later reported that 148,326,583.15 KII was drained across 18 exploit sequences, with part of the funds bridged to BNB Chain through Hyperlane before the halt.

KiiChain stated that the exploit combined an arithmetic underflow in the Cosmos EVM staking precompile's post-delegation balance write-back with additional balance-accounting flaws in the shared Cosmos EVM module. Public descriptions diverged on whether the exploit effectively minted unauthorized KII or only redirected existing balances from victim accounts. KiiChain's v7.4.0 emergency release stated that the chained defects "allowed the attacker to mint and move native KII that the bank ledger never authorized," while later ecosystem analyses described the exploit as a victim-balance redirection that did not increase total supply.

name: TAC
label: Integer Underflow; Ledger Conversion Error; Overwriting Protocol-Controlled Account; Withdrawal Logic Flaw
rootCause:
On August 22, 2026, TAC's bonded staking pool was drained in a flash exploit attributed to a logic flaw in the Cosmos EVM module. Approximately 2.985 billion TAC (28.6% of supply) was moved in a single transaction, with most proceeds bridged to BNB Chain and partially sold for USDT. The chain remains halted, and recovery plans involve treasury replacement and targeted account edits.

The root cause was an unchecked integer underflow and spendable-balance mismatch in the Cosmos EVM module. Delegating locked/vesting tokens from an Ethereum-compatible account incorrectly deducted from zero spendable balance, causing a subtraction wraparound that enabled an attacker contract to grant itself an unwarranted surplus. Protocol-controlled account protection failed to block this path, allowing the bonded staking pool to be emptied without minting new tokens.

name: The Sandbox
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
The Sandbox's cross-chain SAND bridge on Base and BNB Chain was exploited using a misconfigured approveAndCall function, enabling an attacker to hijack LayerZero delegate permissions and mint unbacked SAND tokens. Although billions in tokens were created, only about $675,000 was extracted before the bridges were halted.

The approveAndCall function in the Base SAND OFT contract permitted arbitrary calls as the token, allowing an attacker to hijack bridge delegate permissions. This enabled the attacker to bypass verification by reconfiguring the LayerZero delegate stack, self-attest messages, and mint unbacked SAND without genuine supply backing.

name: MANTRA Chain
label: Arithmetic Error; Integer Underflow; Upstream Dependency Vulnerability
rootCause:
MANTRA Chain halted block production between Aug. 20 and Aug. 22, 2026 after attackers exploited a reported arithmetic flaw in the upstream Cosmos EVM dependency used by the network’s EVM module. Public postmortem reporting states that about 720.9 million MANTRA tokens were moved from a burn address and a legacy multisig wallet, with an estimated impact near $3.6 million and no reported user fund losses.

MANTRA’s published postmortem summaries and subsequent reporting attribute the incident to an arithmetic flaw in the upstream cosmos/evm dependency. The reported vulnerable balance-deduction logic used unsigned integer arithmetic without validating that an account balance could safely cover the subtraction, allowing underflow behavior during balance updates. The exact vulnerable source revision and deployed code path were not independently verified from primary repository evidence during research.

name: Allbridge
label: Forged cross-chain message; Missing mint/balance verification; Bridge logic flaw (CCTP integration)
rootCause:
On August 19, 2026, Allbridge’s Base cross-chain USDC router was exploited for approximately $190,000. The attacker forged a Circle CCTP message weeks before the attack, then combined it with a flash loan to withdraw unbacked USDC, exploiting the bridge contract’s failure to properly verify the underlying mint and balance change.

Allbridge’s Base router trusted Circle CCTP attestations as proof of a valid cross-chain USDC deposit without independently verifying an actual mint or increase in balance. The lack of sender, recipient, and mint validation allowed a forged but attestable message to be redeemed for real funds when router liquidity was sufficient.

name: BounceBit
label: Access Control; Authorization Logic Flaw
rootCause:
BounceBit Chain suffered a protocol-level authorization exploit on August 19,20, 2026, allowing an attacker to transfer 286.5 million BB tokens (~$3 million) from nine mainnet accounts. The exploit forced the permanent shutdown and planned migration of assets to BNB Chain.

A flawed authorization check in BounceBit Chain's Evmos-based vesting/account lock module allowed unauthorized transfers. Attackers could select any source account for fund movement, bypassing intended access verification.

name: Maya Protocol
label: Protocol Logic; Withdrawal Logic Flaw
rootCause:
MAYAChain halted on 2026-08-18 after a six-bug withdrawal and accounting exploit let an attacker inflate a thin CACAO pool, withdraw real reserves, and cause about $1.7 million in direct losses.

A withdrawal compensation path treated a legitimate outbound transfer as missing, calculated an uncapped CACAO subsidy against a thin pool, and failed to roll back the inflated pool credit when the reserve transfer could not be funded.

name: Bodega Market
label: Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Bodega Market's incident on 14 August 2026 remains classified by industry catalogues as oracle manipulation, with a reported loss of $3,600. No technical details, exploit transactions, or root-cause disclosure have been published. The mechanism and response are unknown.

The incident is classified as 'oracle manipulation' in multiple catalogues, but the specific exploit mechanism, affected price feed, and contract vulnerability are undocumented.

name: Harmony
label: Bridge Exploit; Cross-Shard Receipt Replay-Protected Flaw
rootCause:
On August 11, 2026, Harmony's cross-shard protocol was exploited by replaying forged receipt proofs, enabling attackers to mint over two trillion ONE tokens. While the printed token total was massive, the realized market loss was about $3.2 million before Harmony rolled back the affected blocks and deployed a patch to fix the core chain-level logic flaw.

The replay-protection check for cross-shard receipts relied on mutable, unauthenticated Merkle proof fields (ShardID, BlockNum) instead of the committee-signed source block header. This allowed attackers to alter valid already-spent receipts to evade single-use enforcement and repeatedly mint new tokens from the same proof.

name: Coinsbuy
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
On August 9, 2026, Coinsbuy, a centralized payments provider, suffered a cross-chain attack draining over $7.9 million from hot wallets on Ethereum and Tron. Attackers exploited privileged access, quickly laundering stolen assets through swap services and privacy networks. Coinsbuy replenished client funds from reserves, but the root cause remains undisclosed.

The attack stemmed from unauthorized access to Coinsbuy's privileged wallet infrastructure, likely at the hot-wallet key management or admin controls layer. The exact technical breach (key compromise, admin session hijack, or internal control failure) has not been publicly confirmed or detailed by the company.

name: Coreum Bridge
label: Bridge Exploit; Bridge Logic Flaw
rootCause:
On 9 August 2026, the Coreum Bridge connecting XRPL and the tx blockchain (formerly Coreum) was exploited, resulting in a loss of about 200,000 XRP. The attacker exploited a flaw in the bridge's relayer deposit verification logic, allowing fake deposits to trigger legitimate XRP withdrawals.

The bridge's relayer verification software accepted deposit memos without confirming actual XRP transfers to the bridge reserve address, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

name: USM
label: Arithmetic Error; Token & Share Accounting; Split-Redemption Flaw
rootCause:
On 9 August 2026, the USM protocol on Ethereum Mainnet lost approximately 70.83 ETH (~$136,000) when an attacker exploited a flaw in the FUM redemption logic. By splitting the redemption into 64 small transactions, the attacker bypassed the contract's intended pricing mechanism and extracted more ETH than would have been possible with a single call.

The USM contract's ethFromDefund() function used an arithmetic mean pricing formula that was not invariant under split transactions. This allowed the attacker to receive a higher total payout by splitting one large redemption into multiple smaller redemptions, which the protocol did not prevent or account for.

name: Atomic Green
label: Signature Replay; Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Atomic Green was exploited on Arbitrum One on August 8, 2026, resulting in a loss of approximately $29,984 in USDC. The exploit involved signature replay that allowed unauthorized burns of Uniswap V3 LP positions under manipulated pricing.

The exploit was possible due to missing bindings in the signature digest, allowing a manager's signature to be replayed across multiple Uniswap V3 LP position IDs. The protocol failed to include position ID, nonce, deadline, chain ID, and other contextual information within the signed message, enabling unauthorized actions.

name: Oraichain
label: Bridge Exploit; Unbacked Cross-Chain Mint; Message Verification Failure
rootCause:
Oraichain halted its network on 2026-08-09 after a vulnerability in an EVM cross-chain transfer path enabled unauthorized ORAI minting. Public reporting confirms bridge and interface restrictions, planned burns of unauthorized balances, and ongoing recovery coordination with exchanges, but the exact exploit transactions and total unauthorized mint quantity remain undisclosed.

Public incident statements attribute the incident to a vulnerability in an EVM cross-chain transfer path that enabled unauthorized ORAI minting. Available evidence supports a message verification or bridge authorization failure, but the vulnerable contract, precise validation flaw, exploit transactions, and full mint arithmetic have not been publicly disclosed.

name: Ravencoin
label: Forged Block Insertion; Input Validation; Consensus Logic Flaw
rootCause:
Ravencoin suffered a consensus-level vulnerability in August 2026 that allowed attackers to forge invalid blocks by manipulating the block header, disrupting the network and prompting a coordinated chain recovery and emergency software patch. No direct user balance loss has been established, but the incident triggered a major chain reorganization and significant market impact.

Ravencoin’s KAWPOW mining code did not validate that the nHeight field in a block header matched the block’s true position, allowing attackers to bypass the full proof of work and forge blocks. This broke the protocol’s core security assumption and led to multiple invalid blocks being appended to the main chain.

name: Hyperliquid Malaysia Community Treasury
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
On August 6, 2026, the Hyperliquid Malaysia community treasury suffered a private key compromise on Solana. No confirmed transaction or loss figure has been published. The incident affected a local group's wallet and not the Hyperliquid trading protocol itself.

The incident was caused by the compromise of the private key controlling the Hyperliquid Malaysia community treasury wallet. The reviewed statements do not confirm exactly how the key was obtained or what method enabled the attacker to access the wallet.

name: Panther Protocol
label: Governance Attack; Malicious Proposal
rootCause:
Panther Protocol’s Base deployment was exploited on 6 August 2026 through a malicious governance proposal using the Reality.eth module, allowing an attacker to drain approximately 5.12 million ZKP tokens and 0.12 ETH. No user funds were affected.

The Reality.eth governance module on Panther Base allowed anyone to submit and self-answer a governance proposal. Its attack path was unopposed due to missing safety checks, enabling proxy upgrades and fund draining. The module was not disabled on Base when no active DAO proposals existed.

name: RRWallet
label: Key Compromise; Weak Key Generation
rootCause:
RRWallet, a Bitcoin wallet app, was exploited on August 6, 2026, losing around $2 million after attackers brute-forced private keys generated by a weak random number generator in the CryptoJS library. The vulnerable recovery phrases could be predicted, leaving all wallets created by RRWallet at risk. No patch was released, and users are advised to migrate funds immediately.

RRWallet used CryptoJS.lib.WordArray.random(), a weak random number generator seeded by Math.random(), to generate wallet recovery phrases. This produced insufficient entropy (search space ~2^39,2^47 rather than 2^128+), making private keys brute-forceable. The app was discontinued and unrepaired.

name: KITE Foundation
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
KITE Foundation detected and contained a private-key compromise on Ethereum in August 2026, pausing all token transfers and migrating to a new contract. Despite aggregator estimates of $13.3M in value at risk, multiple independent news and official statements confirm there was no realized loss,the affected addresses were excluded during the migration, and no Foundation or user tokens were irretrievably transferred.

Compromise of one or more private keys controlling KITE Foundation Ethereum wallets enabled potential unauthorized token transfers. Immediate detection and transfer pause contained the incident before any tokens left Foundation or user custody.

name: Unistreets LaunchpadFactoryAuto
label: Access Control; Arbitrary External Call; Confused Deputy
rootCause:
Unistreets' LaunchpadFactoryAuto contract was exploited on Ethereum on 5 August 2026, resulting in the loss of 17,743 USDC, a small amount of WETH, and launched memecoin LP assets. Attackers abused arbitrary calldata injection to gain operator rights over all factory-held Uniswap v4 LP positions and drain liquidity in two coordinated transactions.

The LaunchpadFactoryAuto contract allowed user-supplied calldata blobs to be forwarded unchecked to PositionManager.multicall(), enabling attackers to inject setApprovalForAll calls that gave exploit contracts operator authority over every factory-owned liquidity position. This let them burn and drain these positions directly.

name: RISEx
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
RISEx disclosed an unauthorized withdrawal of 673,011.56 USDC from an XLP treasury strategy on 2026-08-03. Public statements attribute the loss to a vault configuration error introduced during deployment of an RWA-linked strategy rather than a confirmed flaw in the exchange matching engine or core perpetuals protocol.

Public disclosures describe a misconfigured XLP treasury RWA strategy that allowed an unauthorized withdrawal of 673,011.56 USDC. The exact contract, configuration parameter, and transaction sequence have not been publicly documented, so the specific access-control or authorization failure remains unverified.

name: LOOPSDAO
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
LOOPSDAO’s LpdFi protocol on BNB Chain was exploited on August 2, 2026, through flash-loan powered spot price manipulation of its LPD/USDC pool. The attacker opened a massively inflated interest-bearing position and claimed disproportionate rewards, draining approximately $690,000.

The protocol calculated LPD token prices based on the instantaneous reserves of a thin PancakeSwap pool, with no TWAP, liquidity threshold, or deviation bounds. Interest accrual used a discrete issue index, enabling a full period's yield to be credited after only a nominal delay.

name: MOKE
label: Spot Price Manipulation; Stale LP Dividend Accounting
rootCause:
The MOKE protocol on BNB Chain was exploited on August 2, 2026, resulting in a loss of approximately $906,800. The attack combined manipulation of spot-price oracles with a flaw in LP dividend accounting, allowing the attacker to claim inflated rewards across duplicated LP records.

MOKE’s vulnerable contracts allowed spot price manipulation to inflate released token rewards, and failed to synchronize LP dividend accounting, letting duplicated records accumulate and enabling unbacked claims.

name: Coldcard
label: Weak seed generation; Key compromise; Bypassed hardware RNG
rootCause:
Between July 30 and August 4, 2026, a firmware flaw in the Coldcard hardware wallet permitted attackers to brute-force weakly generated Bitcoin seeds, resulting in losses exceeding $116 million. The incident stemmed from a software bug that bypassed hardware-based entropy during wallet seed generation.

A build configuration error in Coldcard firmware released March 2021 caused the device to generate wallet seeds using a weak software-based pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) instead of the intended hardware random number generator, producing seeds with as little as 40 bits of entropy. This made the resulting private keys susceptible to brute-force attacks, enabling attackers to drain funds from affected addresses without physical access to the devices.

name: Set Protocol
label: TOCTOU (time-of-check/time-of-use) accounting gap; Manager-controlled state mutation (pre-issue hook); Valuation parameter manipulation
rootCause:
On July 30, 2026, Set Protocol was exploited on Ethereum Mainnet through a time-of-check/time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerability in the ExchangeIssuance contract. The attacker used a manager-controlled hook to inflate valuation data after asset quoting but before transfer, draining over $9,600 in multi-asset value, including LINK, UNI, AAVE, MKR, WBTC, and USDC.

The ExchangeIssuance contract calculated required asset values for issuance, then called an external manager hook that could mutate those parameters before final asset transfer. This TOCTOU gap allowed malicious manager contracts to alter key values, causing excess assets to be issued.

name: Swan Treasury
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
On July 30, 2026, Swan Treasury suffered a $625,246 loss on BNB Chain due to a compromised off-chain signer key. The attacker forged a purchase order, using a flash loan and manipulated the discount parameter to buy STY tokens at one-hundredth the intended price, extracting over 871,000 STY and swiftly converting to USDT.

The loss was caused by a compromised off-chain signing key and the absence of on-chain bounds on critical economic parameters. The buy() function authenticated with the signer address but allowed arbitrary discount values, enabling the attacker to mint tokens at an extreme discount.

name: Crypto DAO
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
Crypto DAO's Pro token contract on BNB Chain was exploited on July 28, 2026 due to a publicly accessible vault function with missing access controls. While headlines cited an $8.2 million loss, evidence-supported attacker profits were closer to $52,000. The incident reflects a recurring pattern of basic access-control failures on BNB Chain.

A vault function in the Pro token contract lacked access checks, allowing any address to call the function and drain funds.

name: LULA
label: Access Control; Reserve Manipulation; Flash Loan
rootCause:
LULA on BNB Chain lost about $578,000 on 2026-07-28 after an attacker abused a privileged recycle() path that could transfer tokens directly out of a PancakeSwap V2 pair and immediately resynchronize reserves with sync(). The attacker combined the reserve rewrite primitive with large flash-loan-backed swaps to distort the LULA/USDT pool price and extract USDT.

Public incident analyses and the checked exploit transaction indicate that LULA exposed an attacker-reachable path to a privileged recycle() function. The function reportedly allowed the Rental contract to transfer LULA directly out of the PancakeSwap V2 pair through an internal balance update and then call sync(), causing the AMM to adopt manipulated balances as official reserves. Repeated reserve reductions pushed the LULA side of the pool close to zero while the USDT side remained large, allowing the attacker to drain USDT at a severely distorted exchange rate.

name: ChainConnect
label: Missing sender verification in callback; Access Control
rootCause:
ChainConnect suffered an exploit on July 26, 2026, due to a missing sender-verification check in its Alien Proxy callback, enabling an unauthorized attacker to mint unbacked tokens and bridge them to EVM chains. About $650,000 was drained, but ~82.9% (~$615,000) was returned, with the remainder kept as a whitehat bounty.

Missing sender-verification in the ProxyMultiVaultAlien_V10.onCheckAccumulatedFee callback allowed unauthorized minting and bridging of unbacked Alien TIP-3 tokens.

name: Garden
label: Frontend Compromise; Database Breach
rootCause:
Garden Finance lost approximately $450,000 USDT on July 26, 2026, when an independent solver's off-chain database was breached. The attacker injected fraudulent swap entries, causing HTLC contracts across Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum One, and BNB Chain to release solver-held funds. No user deposits or protocol contracts were directly compromised.

Compromise of an independent solver’s off-chain database allowed the attacker to inject fraudulent swap records. The solver’s automated reconciliation trusted these records, releasing funds from HTLC contracts without actual counterparties. Garden protocol contracts and user funds remained unaffected.

name: WEMIX.FI Lend
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
WEMIX.FI Lend suffered an access control incident on WEMIX3.0 on 2026-07-26 after an attacker obtained privileged authority over a WEMIX$-related contract. The attacker minted unauthorized WEMIX$ tokens, swapped part of the supply into WEMIX and USDC.e, and bridged assets to other chains. Public reporting consistently places the realized extraction near $724,000 to $737,000, but the exact compromise path and affected contract addresses remain undisclosed.

Public disclosures describe a compromise of owner or administrator authority over a WEMIX$-related contract that enabled unauthorized token minting and liquidity extraction. The precise initial compromise mechanism, including whether it involved stolen keys, signer infrastructure, upgrade permissions, or a contract-level authorization flaw, was not publicly established in the consulted evidence.

name: Bankr
label: Social Engineering; Social Account Takeover
rootCause:
On 2026-07-25, Bankr's official @bankrbot X account was reportedly compromised and used to post a fake airdrop link. Public incident tracking associated the event with a reported $479,885 loss on Base, and Bankr later said no Bankr contract vulnerability or infrastructure breach was involved.

Available evidence indicates unauthorized takeover of Bankr's official @bankrbot X account. The attacker used that trusted social identity to publish a fake airdrop link. Bankr later said its infrastructure and product were not compromised, and no Bankr smart contract bug has been publicly identified for this event. The exact X-account compromise path and the wallet-level transaction sequence behind the reported $479,885 Base loss remain unpublished.

name: Projekt GREEN/GOLD Reward Vault
label: Input Validation; Reward Logic Flaw
rootCause:
The Projekt GREEN/GOLD reward vault on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited on July 25, 2026, for approximately $560,000 (301.7 ETH). The root cause was insufficient input validation in the rewards purchase tracking logic, allowing an attacker to inflate vault balances using flash liquidity and Uniswap operations.

Missing input validation in the reward allocation logic allowed balance inflations via flash liquidity and Uniswap V2 operations, leading to unauthorized reward withdrawals.

name: Triple-A
label: Social engineering; Hot wallet access compromise
rootCause:
Triple-A's operational treasury was breached on July 24,25, 2026, through a social engineering attack that enabled unauthorized access to hot wallets on multiple chains. Stolen funds, totaling up to $11.8 million, were consolidated on Ethereum and swapped to DAI. No client funds were affected.

Attackers gained access to credentials for Triple-A's operational wallets via a sophisticated social engineering attack targeting engineering personnel. This led to full compromise of the wallet management environment rather than a smart contract or infrastructure flaw.

name: Lien Finance
label: Input Validation; Missing Input Validation
rootCause:
On 23 July 2026, Lien Finance on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited via a permissionless bond group registration flaw and inadequate input validation that enabled an attacker to mint unbacked bond tokens, manipulate OTC pool pricing, and extract approximately $542,144 in USDC from protocol liquidity pools.

The Lien protocol failed to adequately validate bond group registration and exchange logic in its GeneralizedDotc OTC pools. The bond group registration was permissionless, and the rate calculation function did not check for the economic legitimacy of new bond groups, enabling arbitrary creation and redemption of unbacked bond tokens.

name: Solido Cash
label: Oracle Misconfiguration; Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Solido Cash was exploited on Supra on July 23, 2026, when a misconfigured oracle fallback assigned collateral tokens a value of $1 each, enabling attackers to mint synthetic tokens against inflated collateral. The incident resulted in losses of approximately $900,000, with most proceeds transferred to centralized exchanges.

A misconfigured oracle fallback assigned an inflated $1 valuation to collateral tokens, allowing attackers to mint synthetic assets against value that did not exist. This overvaluation enabled draining protocol liquidity.

name: AFX Trade
label: Private Key Compromise; Social Engineering; Supply Chain Attack
rootCause:
AFX Trade's AFX-operated custody bridge released 24,150,000 USDC on Arbitrum on 2026-07-22 after a multi-stage intrusion reached validator-related infrastructure and produced enough real signing authority to satisfy the bridge's withdrawal rules.

AFX's 2026-07-25 disclosure describes a supply chain intrusion that began when a developer cloned a malicious repository after a Telegram contact, then spread through AFX's JFrog environment and internal systems until it reached validator-related infrastructure. The bridge accepted a withdrawal that carried sufficient real signing authority under its configured quorum rules. No public evidence in the consulted materials establishes a smart-contract logic bug in the bridge verifier.

name: Verus-Ethereum Bridge
label: Bridge Exploit; Forged Proof
rootCause:
On July 23, 2026, the Verus-Ethereum Bridge was exploited for approximately $7.54 million. The attacker forged import proofs using poisoned notarization data from Verus, causing the Ethereum bridge contract to release funds without proper backing on the source chain.

Discrepant interpretation of notarization data between Verus and Ethereum allowed an attacker to inject a malicious state root. The Ethereum bridge contract subsequently relied on this forged checkpoint, failing to verify that payout amounts matched value exported from Verus.

name: Zilliqa
label: Nonce bias in Schnorr signature (weak key exposure); Private key recovery via lattice reduction
rootCause:
The Zilliqa legacy chain suffered a critical key exposure incident affecting Ledger hardware wallets, enabling attackers to reconstruct private keys from biased Schnorr signatures. 683,130,969.66 ZIL was stolen across 66 confirmed theft transactions between March and July 2026, with legacy transactions paused for migration and recovery.

A nonce copying defect in the Zilliqa Ledger app for Schnorr signatures biased the nonce's high 64 bits to zero, enabling private key recovery from just four or five publicly posted signatures.

name: 42DAO Balance Protocol
label: Oracle Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
42DAO's Balance Coin (BLC) on BNB Chain was reported exploited on 2026-07-21 after a manipulated BTCB spot price entered the protocol's liquidation path, with public loss estimates around $912,000 to $915,000 and a brief depeg to near $0.0013.

Public analyses indicate that 42DAO's liquidation path accepted an abnormally low BTCB spot price without deviation checks, minimum price protections, or liquidation delay, so a manipulated price could drive liquidations or other accounting actions at a false valuation.

name: FlashTrade
label: Missing Input Validation; PDA (Program Derived Address) Validation Flaw
rootCause:
FlashTrade, a Solana-based perpetuals DEX, was exploited on July 21, 2026 after insufficient validation of the buffer account in MagicBlock's undelegation logic. A forged account bypassed program-derived address checks, enabling an unauthorized withdrawal of ~$98,000 USDC. The incident was detected within minutes and operations paused. All users were reimbursed and the vulnerable SDK was rapidly patched.

The MagicBlock SDK's undelegation instruction accepted attacker-supplied buffer accounts without verifying that they matched the canonical program-derived address (PDA). This omission enabled a forged account to bypass intended authentication and withdraw funds.

name: Wanchain Cardano Bridge
label: Signature Verification Flaw; Non-injective Message Encoding; Input Validation
rootCause:
The Wanchain Cardano bridge was exploited on July 20, 2026, due to a fundamental flaw in its Plutus validator's message encoding. Attackers replayed a legitimate BNB Chain withdrawal signature to drain approximately $10 million in NIGHT tokens. Most stolen tokens were quickly liquidated and no confirmed recovery has been published.

The TreasuryCheck validator on Cardano used raw concatenation of variable-length redeemer fields without explicit delimiters or length prefixes. This allowed different input sets to produce identical byte sequences, enabling attackers to replay a signature from a legitimate withdrawal on BNB Chain and drain much larger sums on Cardano.

name: Allbridge Core
label: Input Validation; Logic Error
rootCause:
On July 19, 2026, Allbridge Core's Solana stablecoin bridge was exploited for $1.65M. The attacker abused a missing check that allowed the same pool account to be passed as both sender and receiver in a swap, corrupting the protocol's internal accounting and enabling outsized withdrawals.

The Solana program for Allbridge Core failed to validate that the send and receive pool account addresses in the swap instruction were distinct. When the same account was used in both roles, Solana instantiated two local mutable objects from the same on-chain state. Only the second object (receive leg) was ultimately written back, so the send leg's critical accounting changes were silently discarded. This created a mismatch between the pool's internal records and actual token balances, which the attacker exploited.

name: Across Protocol
label: Bridge Exploit; Spoofed Event Log
rootCause:
Across's Solana relayer accepted forged deposit events and advanced about $4.5 million in relayer capital before Solana routing was paused and later rerouted through CCTP. User funds were reportedly unaffected, but the final net loss and recovery are still not fully reconciled.

The offchain Solana relayer trusted event-shaped inner instructions as real deposits after matching the Across program id and event-authority PDA, but it did not fully verify the Anchor event discriminator or reject failed transactions. That let a reverted transaction look like a valid deposit to the relayer.

name: FlyCow
label: Incorrect Share Accounting; Reserve Manipulation; Mid-swap forced reserve sync
rootCause:
On July 17, 2026, the FlyCow (FCOW) token contract on BNB Chain was exploited via reserve manipulation of its PancakeSwap pair, resulting in a confirmed loss of roughly $65,258 USDT and BNB. The exploit abused a token transfer path that burned tokens from the liquidity pair and forcibly updated reserves during swap calculations.

The FCOW token's transfer logic allowed unauthorized burns and an immediate sync of the PancakeSwap FCOW/USDT pair during transferFrom() into the pair. This broke the DEX router's assumption that reserves would remain stable throughout the swap, enabling price distortion and draining the pool.

name: CrowdRingCircle
label: Logic Error; Incorrect Share Accounting
rootCause:
CrowdRingCircle was exploited on BNB Chain on 16 July 2026 due to a flawed sell-tax burn mechanism in its BEP-20 token, enabling an attacker to drain approximately $209,100 in USDT from the CRC/USDT PancakeSwap V2 pair by corrupting AMM reserves mid-transfer.

The CRC token's _update() function burned tokens directly from the pair's balance and called sync() before crediting the sold principal, causing the AMM pair's cached reserves to reflect an artificially low CRC balance. This let an attacker drain nearly all USDT from the pool using a direct swap against manipulated reserves.

name: DeFiTuna
label: Logic Error; Rounding Error
rootCause:
On July 16, 2026, the Solana-based DeFiTuna protocol lost approximately $570,000 after an attacker exploited a logic flaw in its position health check. The attacker used a manipulated, nearly empty AMM pool and a rounding bug to create and extract unbacked debt, bypassing solvency enforcement.

The vulnerable branch in DeFiTuna's position health check treated any position with asset value rounded to zero as healthy, regardless of outstanding debt. This allowed an attacker to create a debt position where the purported collateral, after a manipulated swap, was so small it rounded to zero, evading proper insolvency detection.

name: BarnBridge
label: Governance Attack; Access Control
rootCause:
On July 15, 2026, an attacker captured governance control of the deprecated BarnBridge protocol on Ethereum, passing proposals and replacing a controller contract. This enabled them to drain about $776K in USDC from roughly 50 user wallets via lingering approvals.

Abandoned but still-powerful governance: BarnBridge’s governance contract retained admin control of lending-integration contracts after protocol deprecation. As total staked governance tokens declined, a hostile attacker cheaply gained enough voting power to pass and execute proposals that swapped the controller for a malicious proxy. This proxy contract then used lingering user USDC approvals to drain their funds.

name: Cascade Liquidity Strategy
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Cascade’s CLS vault on Arbitrum was exploited on 15 July 2026. Attackers manipulated mark prices in a thin-liquidity perpetuals market to force liquidation of vault short positions, resulting in losses of around $1.34 million. The stolen USDC was bridged to Solana, swapped to DAI, and deposited on Ethereum to evade freezing.

The CLS vault's mark price logic allowed attacker-controlled positions in thin markets to artificially inflate prices, forcing liquidation of vault short positions at manipulated levels. No manipulation-resistant oracle or price-sanity checks were built into the contract, leaving it vulnerable to targeted price moves by attackers.

name: Ostium
label: Oracle Manipulation; Private Key Compromise
rootCause:
On July 15, 2026, attackers drained Ostium's liquidity vault for $23.75M by exploiting compromised off-chain credentials controlling price feeds. They submitted validly signed, fabricated price reports, enabling rapid open-close leverage trades, and extracted profits the protocol could not detect.

The attacker obtained the private key for an authorized off-chain price report signer and a registered keeper. The on-chain contracts accepted any validly signed price report from authorized figures, but performed no secondary checks for price plausibility or origin. No anomaly detection or circuit breaker stopped the rapid draining loop.

name: TeleSwap
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
TeleSwap's Bitcoin bridge was exploited on July 15, 2026 after the hot wallet private key was compromised, resulting in losses estimated at $735,000. The attacker withdrew funds directly from the bridge's Bitcoin wallet and laundered assets using cross-chain swaps and Tornado Cash. TeleSwap did not publicly disclose the incident for at least five days.

The incident resulted from compromise of TeleSwap's Bitcoin hot wallet private key, which allowed direct unauthorized withdrawals from custody. The bridge relied on operational key security rather than on-chain or contract-level protections.

name: Drips Network
label: Arithmetic Error; Unsafe Integer Conversion
rootCause:
Drips Network suffered a loss of approximately 24,883 DAI on Ethereum Mainnet due to an unsafe integer conversion in the DaiDripsHub contract's give() function. The attacker exploited a silent uint128 to int128 cast that inverted transfer direction, draining the reserve via a crafted call.

Unsafe casting from uint128 to int128 in DaiDripsHub.give(address,uint128), enabling a sign flip that reversed transfer direction and allowed attackers to drain the DAI reserve.

name: Chi Protocol
label: Logic Error; Redeem Logic Flaw
rootCause:
On July 13, 2026, Chi Protocol on Ethereum Mainnet lost approximately $8,500 due to a logic flaw in its redemption mechanism. The attacker bought depegged USC tokens cheaply, then redeemed them for full-value collateral using a burn() logic error.

The ArbitrageV5 contract's burn() function allowed users to redeem USC stablecoins for collateral at a fixed $1 rate without checking if the token was still pegged at $1, letting an attacker profit by redeeming depegged tokens for more collateral than they were worth.

name: Lumi Finance
label: Input Validation; Signature Verification Flaw
rootCause:
Lumi Finance on Arbitrum One was exploited on July 13, 2026, resulting in the loss of approximately $270,000 from individual user smart accounts. The breach was caused by a flaw in validation logic allowing ERC-20 token approvals during the ERC-4337 account abstraction validation phase, granting attackers mass token allowances and enabling rapid theft.

The Sodium smart account contract failed to enforce that validation phase code was strictly side-effect free. As a result, attacker-controlled paymasters induced ERC-20 token approvals during UserOperation validation, granting token allowances without user signatures or intent. This broke a key ERC-4337 invariant and enabled mass theft.

name: PHX
label: Logic Error; Incorrect Share Accounting; Custom Token Burn Sync Issue
rootCause:
On July 12, 2026, the PHX token contract on BNB Chain was exploited for 156.205683367 WBNB (≈$89,532), after an attacker manipulated PancakeSwap pool reserves via the token's flawed burn-and-sync logic in a flash-loan-aided transaction.

A sell transfer on the PHX token burned tokens directly from the PancakeSwap PHX/WBNB pair, then synced reserves before crediting the net sell amount. This sequence let the attacker set an artificial reserve baseline and drain nearly all WBNB at a mispriced swap, violating AMM invariants.

name: BlueMove DEX
label: Liquidity-provider share accounting bug; Cross-version reserve desynchronization
rootCause:
BlueMove DEX was exploited on Sui on 11 July 2026 through an LP token accounting vulnerability, draining approximately $525,000 worth of assets across nearly 400 liquidity pools. Funds were converted and moved out of Sui before pools were frozen, enabling continued token drainage from broken pools.

A liquidity-provider share accounting bug in BlueMove's legacy AMM implementation allowed an attacker to inflate LP token balances and withdraw more assets than they should have held. Cross-version desynchronization further exposed nearly 400 pools, which were left unfrozen after the main exploit.

name: Bonzo Finance
label: Oracle Manipulation; Signature Abuse
rootCause:
On July 11, 2026, Bonzo Lend on Hedera suffered a $9.05M loss when Supra's oracle verifier allowed an attacker to publish a forged SAUCE price update with a zeroed signature, enabling massive undercollateralized borrowing.

Supra's on-chain oracle verifier failed to reject zeroed BLS signature and public key inputs when given a committee ID outside the valid range. This let the Hedera pairing precompile accept a mathematically valid but non-authorized signature, allowing an attacker to submit a manipulated price update.

name: BFB Token
label: Logic Error; Zero-value transferFrom abuse; Price-defense pool burn; Flash loans
rootCause:
BFB Token was exploited on BNB Chain on July 8, 2026, due to zero-value transfer abuse in its price-defense logic. The attacker drained approximately 350.62 WBNB (~$197,800) by repeatedly triggering reserve burns in the PancakeSwap pool without expending tokens.

The BFBToken contract failed to check transfer amount before executing price-defense side effects. This enabled repeated zero-value transferFrom() calls,each triggering reserve burns,allowing pool depletion by an attacker without genuine token movement or value input.

name: BonkDAO
label: Governance Attack
rootCause:
On July 6, 2026, BonkDAO's treasury on Solana was drained of roughly $21.2M worth of BONK tokens after an attacker bought ~$4.4M of BONK to pass a malicious proposal. Flawed governance rules allowed instant asset movement by vote, with no timelock or secondary sign-off.

BonkDAO's governance was configured with a quorum threshold priced below the value of its treasury (1% of BONK supply), no timelock, and allowed direct treasury transfers by vote alone. The attacker could cheaply acquire enough BONK to control the vote and execute asset movement in the same transaction, bypassing any review or intervention.

name: Lazy Summer Protocol
label: Logic Error; Price Manipulation
rootCause:
On July 6, 2026, Lazy Summer Protocol (Summer.fi) lost $6.04M when an attacker inflated two USDC vault share prices by donating overvalued Silo tokens to a still-active Ark pending removal. The stale Ark had its deposit cap set to zero nine months earlier but remained in the vault's asset calculation, allowing the attacker to withdraw much more than deposited.

A strategy adapter (Ark) holding impaired Silo "Varlamore USDC Growth" tokens was capped for offboarding but never fully removed. The vault's NAV still counted these tokens at their pre-collapse valuation, permitting share-price manipulation via donation of cheap, overvalued tokens.

name: Hinkal
label: Logic Error
rootCause:
On July 2, 2026, Hinkal's shielded-pool protocol on Ethereum was exploited for about $800K in a double-spend attack. The incident resulted from a legacy note format flaw that allowed a single deposit to be withdrawn multiple times, with proceeds laundered through Tornado Cash and THORChain.

The legacy note format permitted multiple valid nullifiers per deposit because the nullifying key (nk) was only bound through its product with a random value, rather than directly. This weak binding enabled one deposit to be spent repeatedly, as the contract delegated nullifier uniqueness enforcement entirely to the zero-knowledge circuit rather than an independent on-chain check.

name: Edel Finance
label: Collateral Exchange-Rate Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation; Flash Loan
rootCause:
Edel Finance suffered a $403,000 loss on Ethereum after an attacker manipulated the wGOOGLx wrapper exchange rate, inflating collateral value by about 78× using flash loans. The lending protocol was left with bad debt, and funds were moved to Tornado Cash.

Edel Finance relied on an internal wrapper exchange rate (wGOOGLx/GOOGLx) that was manipulable by flash-loan cycles. The protocol did not constrain rapid exchange-rate changes or validate the backing behind collateral valuation. Chainlink price feeds remained correct, but the ERC-4626 vault's assets-per-share ratio was vulnerable.

name: AIDC
label: Logic Error; Arithmetic Error; Burn Mechanism Flaw
rootCause:
AIDC token was exploited on BNB Chain on June 28, 2026, via a logic flaw in its sell/burn accounting, allowing an attacker to drain approximately 220 WBNB (~$121,000) from its PancakeSwap liquidity pool. The burn logic erroneously destroyed tokens from the pool rather than the seller, breaking AMM invariants.

AIDC's _sellTransfer() and _executeAccumulatedBurn() functions deferred burn accounting and mistakenly burned tokens from the AMM liquidity pool balance, allowing reserves to be artificially compressed while WBNB backing remained, facilitating extraction of greatly inflated WBNB.

name: Lixir Finance
label: Broken permit signature validation; Input validation flaw
rootCause:
On 25 June 2026, Lixir Finance's Ethereum vault system was exploited via a forged permit signature vulnerability. The attacker reused a single EIP-2612 signature to gain fraudulent approvals, draining over $12,300 in USDC, USDT, ETH, and LIX from multiple vault-share contracts.

Lixir's custom permit implementation failed to check that the recovered signer matched the provided owner. This enabled arbitrary approvals via forged signatures, allowing unauthorized withdrawal of vault-share assets.

name: Nomic
label: Bridge Exploit; Double Spend; Unbacked Mint
rootCause:
A June 25 Nomic forwarding bug minted 40.650602 nBTC without BTC backing and left Osmosis allBTC short until a September freeze and recovery proposal.

A public forensic reconstruction attributes the mint to a Nomic forwarding path that did not verify packet sender authorization and allowed escrow balance aliasing, so 25 self-referential ICS-20 packets minted nBTC without consuming new BTC backing.

name: Ocean Protocol
label: Logic Error; Deposit Logic Flaw
rootCause:
Ocean Protocol's BPool/SideStaking pools on Polygon were exploited on June 25, 2026, using a logic flaw in single-sided join/exit accounting. The attacker drained about 127,861 mOCEAN, valued at roughly $11.8K, by repeatedly minting and burning pool shares across multiple Ocean pools, extracting more mOCEAN than contributed.

A broken accounting invariant in Ocean Protocol's BPool implementation allowed a single-sided join followed by a single-sided exit to mint and redeem pool shares at mismatched rates, amplified by SideStaking's automatic datatoken co-staking. The attacker could repeatedly increase their base-token balance through this sequence.

name: Polymarket International
label: Frontend Compromise
rootCause:
Polymarket International's frontend was compromised by a supply-chain attack on 25 June 2026, resulting in the theft of approximately $2.94,$3.1 million in PUSD from user wallets on Polygon. Malicious JavaScript injected through a third-party vendor dependency redirected user approvals, draining funds. Smart contracts and backend infrastructure were not affected. Polymarket removed the vendor dependency and pledged full reimbursement, but the compromised dependency and primary chain transaction evidence remain undisclosed.

A third-party vendor dependency loaded by Polymarket's frontend was compromised, allowing an attacker to inject malicious JavaScript. This script hijacked wallet approval flows in the user browser, prompting victims to approve transfers to attacker-controlled addresses. The provenance of delivered frontend code was not independently verified before execution.

name: DLMC
label: Spot Price Manipulation; Flash Loan Exploit; Referral/Reward Logic Flaw
rootCause:
DLMC on BNB Chain lost ~$222,600 USDT in a flash-loan driven spot price manipulation exploit. The attacker inflated the token price by flash-swapping USDT, manipulating the protocol’s self-pricing logic, and redeeming referral rewards at the synthetic price to drain the treasury.

The protocol’s internal price calculation used USDT reserves divided by externally circulating supply, excluding most freshly minted DLMC tokens held by the contract itself. This allowed flash-loan deposits to inflate the price, enabling extraction of referral rewards at artificially high value.

name: Royal.io
label: ERC1155 zero-amount batch transfer; Incorrect share accounting; Custom balance desynchronization
rootCause:
On June 23, 2026, Royal.io’s legacy Polygon royalties contract was exploited via a zero-amount ERC1155 batch transfer that inflated tier accounting, causing an unauthorized USDC withdrawal of about $261,000. The root cause was inconsistent custom share accounting in the Royal1155LDA contract.

The Royal1155LDA contract failed to check and process nonzero transfer amounts in its custom ownership accounting hook. Zero-amount batch transfers could incorrectly increment the recipient's tier balance, inflating pro-rata royalty entitlement without real ERC1155 ownership.

name: SecondFi
label: Ed25519 signing implementation flaw; Signature nonce exposure; Private Key Compromise
rootCause:
A cryptographic flaw in SecondFi's Ed25519 signing implementation enabled attackers to recover user private keys from Cardano transaction data. Approximately $2.4M in ADA was drained from 374 wallets before emergency rescue efforts secured further at-risk funds, and EMURGO permanently discontinued the wallet.

SecondFi's Ed25519 signing code derived the signature nonce only from the public transaction message, omitting the secret prefix required by the Ed25519 standard. This made every signature publicly invertible: anyone could algebraically recover a wallet's private key from standard transaction data. The flaw affected every address that signed with the vulnerable implementation; mere wallet creation was not enough to compromise funds.

name: Quicksilver Zone
label: Forged delegation proofs; Unbacked mint
rootCause:
On 21 June 2026, Quicksilver Zone suffered an exploit involving forged proofs for delegation, allowing an attacker to mint unbacked liquid staking tokens (qATOM, qOSMO) on the Quicksilver chain. The drained value was about $3,500, and the exploit stemmed from a lack of proper proof validation before issuing qAssets.

Failure to authenticate delegation proofs in the interchain liquid staking issuance flow enabled unbacked mints.

name: Taiko
label: Input Validation; Private Key Compromise
rootCause:
On June 21, 2026, Taiko's Ethereum L1 bridge lost approximately $1.7M after an attacker exploited a leaked SGX enclave signing key to forge L2 state proofs. The attacker used the compromised key and unchecked enclave attributes to register a rogue prover, issue fraudulent bridge messages, and drain the protocol. Taiko replenished the loss from treasury, confirming no user funds were lost.

An RSA‑3072 private key used to sign SGX enclave attestations was committed to Taiko’s public GitHub repository. The on-chain attestation contract failed to check enclave DEBUG attributes, allowing an attacker to register a malicious DEBUG-mode prover and forge valid-looking L2 state proofs, leading to repeated unauthorized withdrawals.

name: JaredFromSubway
label: Logic Error; Token Approval Abuse
rootCause:
On June 20, 2026, the JaredFromSubway MEV bot on Ethereum was drained of about $7.5 million in WETH, USDC, and USDT. The attacker constructed a honeypot of fake token contracts and pools, tricking the bot into approving tokens without consuming allowances. These unspent approvals were drained in a single sweep.

The bot's automated trading logic granted token approvals to untrusted, attacker-controlled wrapper contracts and pools without verifying that allowances were actually consumed after trades. These standing permissions persisted, accumulating open exposures that the attacker harvested in a single batch transaction.

name: LABUBU/OLPC
label: Reserve mismatch via amplified deflationary burn; Tokenomics parameter misconfiguration; Destructive interaction with AMM housekeeping functions
rootCause:
LABUBU/OLPC's PancakeSwap V2 pool on BNB Chain was exploited on June 20, 2026, resulting in a $1.12M loss through a reserve mismatch triggered by OLPC's amplified burn mechanism, allowing the attacker to drain LABUBU at distorted prices.

The OLPC token applied an amplified burn on pair-originated transfers, using an unbounded owner-set multiplier decimalsValue, which interacted destructively with PancakeSwap's public skim/sync mechanics, collapsing pool reserves and enabling the attacker to drain LABUBU at mispriced rates.

name: mySwap CL
label: Logic Error; Incorrect Share Accounting
rootCause:
On June 19, 2026, mySwap concentrated liquidity pools on Starknet were exploited using a malicious token, resulting in losses of approximately $305,000. The attacker manipulated pool accounting to withdraw honest LP assets from a dormant protocol vault.

mySwap's accounting logic allowed arbitrary token contracts to be added to its concentrated liquidity pools, trusting their reported balances without strict validation. This let an attacker use a worthless, attacker-controlled token to inflate pool share claims and withdraw real assets from the shared vault.

name: Namada Shielded Pools
label: IBC Transfer Logic Flaw
rootCause:
On June 19, 2026, Namada's Multi-Asset Shielded Pool (MASP) was drained via an IBC transfer logic flaw. Approximately $600,000 in assets,including ATOM, USDC, OSMO, TIA, and NYM,were swept from the privacy pool. The loss was masked at first due to a stale indexer, leaving balances falsely visible.

A flaw in Namada's implementation of IBC transfer logic enabled unauthorized withdrawals from the shielded pool, allowing an attacker to drain assets without proper accounting or verification. The privacy-by-design features and lagging indexer delayed detection.

name: JB
label: Privileged AMM reserve mutation; Spot price manipulation; Burn-and-sync abuse
rootCause:
On June 18, 2026, the JB token contract on BNB Chain was exploited using a flash-loan and reserve-manipulation sequence that abused a privileged token burn and sync function to drain around $50,000 from the JB/USDT PancakeSwap V2 pool. The attacker was able to repeatedly shrink the pool's JB reserve after each sell, enabling further extraction of USDT value in a single transaction.

A privileged function in the JB token contract enabled an authorized route contract to burn tokens directly from the AMM pair and then call sync(), allowing the attacker to repeatedly reset reserves and manipulate the price curve out of normal trading bounds.

name: Little Boy Plus
label: Unauthorized Mint; Reserve Desynchronization; Zero-value transferFrom bypass
rootCause:
On June 18, 2026, Little Boy Plus was exploited on BNB Chain via an unauthorized minting bug. A zero-value transferFrom call bypassed allowance checks in the LBPHashrate contract, enabling the attacker to mint tokens directly into the PancakeSwap pair and desynchronize AMM reserves.
