The attacker drained approximately $377,642 USDT (about 610.5 BNB) through a single flash-loan-fueled swap, with no reported recovery or official mitigation published. Evidence is limited to technical monitoring and incident summaries; no direct block explorer transactions or full contract source are published.

The LBPHashrate contract allowed a zero-value transferFrom call to bypass ERC-20 allowance checks, triggering unauthorized reward minting directly into the AMM pair. This desynchronized the pair's token balance from its tracked reserve, letting the attacker drain USDT via a swap.

name: Aztec Private Rollup Bridge
label: Logic Error; Proof Verification Failure
rootCause:
On June 17, 2026, an attacker drained about 1,158 ETH from Aztec's deprecated Private Rollup Bridge on Ethereum by abusing the legacy escapeHatch(bytes,bytes,bytes) withdrawal path. The immutable rollup deployment accepted a proof whose withdrawal outputs were not correctly bound to the ownership state the proof was supposed to authorize, allowing the attacker to redirect bridge funds to an attacker-controlled address.

The legacy Aztec Private Rollup Bridge trusted escape-hatch proof data whose withdrawal outputs were not sufficiently constrained to the ownership state represented inside the proof system. Public technical analyses described a missing binding between the private join-split state and the public withdrawal recipient consumed by L1 settlement. After verifier success, the RollupProcessor decoded attacker-controlled withdrawal fields from proofData and executed a real ETH withdrawal without an additional ownership assertion.

name: DIP Protocol
label: Swap Logic Flaw; Router-involved transfer double execution
rootCause:
DIP Protocol was exploited on BNB Chain on June 16, 2026, by an attacker who abused a flawed token transfer logic in the DIP contract. The bug allowed double count withdrawal from the DIP-AIC pair, resulting in a loss of approximately 111,098 USDC.

The DIP token's internal _transfer function executed router-involved transfers twice instead of once, leading to a reserve-accounting mismatch that allowed the attacker to drain nearly all DIP liquidity from the pool.

name: Thetanuts Finance
label: Token & Share Accounting; Rounding Error
rootCause:
Thetanuts Finance's deprecated options vault on Ethereum was exploited for $2.1M through a rounding bug in share/claim accounting, allowing free minting and redemption of option tokens. Most funds were recovered by a white-hat.

The legacy vault's mint logic performed integer division that could round deposit amounts to zero under specific low-supply states, enabling attackers to repeatedly mint new option tokens without paying for collateral.

name: Aztec Connect
label: Logic Error; Settlement Boundary Mismatch
rootCause:
On June 14, 2026, an attacker drained roughly $2.15M to $2.19M from Aztec Connect's deprecated RollupProcessorV3 on Ethereum by exploiting a mismatch between zk-proof commitments and Layer 1 settlement accounting. The exploit minted unbacked L2 balances that were later withdrawn as real ETH and ERC20 assets from the immutable legacy bridge.

RollupProcessorV3 trusted a numRealTransactions value that was not fully bound into the proof commitment used by settlement verification. The zk proof committed transaction slots that included attacker-controlled deposit operations, but the Layer 1 settlement loop processed only the first numRealTransactions entries. Deposits placed in later decoded slots minted L2 balances without executing the corresponding decreasePendingDepositBalance() funding checks on Layer 1, enabling withdrawals backed by no real deposit.

name: Axelar,Secret IBC Bridge
label: Bridge Exploit; Unbacked Cross-Chain Mint
rootCause:
On June 10, 2026, the Axelar,Secret IBC Bridge was exploited due to a missing channel validation check, allowing attackers to mint unbacked assets on Secret Network and withdraw genuine reserves from the Axelar bridge. The incident resulted in an estimated $4.67 million loss. No attacker recovery or reimbursement was confirmed as of evidence review.

The Secret-side bridge contract failed to authenticate the legitimate IBC channel on inbound token messages, enabling attackers to mint unbacked Axelar-wrapped assets and redeem them for real bridge reserves.

name: Raydium AMM
label: Logic Error; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
On 10 June 2026, five deprecated Raydium AMM V3 pools on Solana were exploited via a logic flaw in LP mint validation, allowing an attacker to drain $1.34 million by faking LP tokens. No active users or current infrastructure were affected; Raydium pledged full reimbursement from protocol treasury.

The legacy AMM V3 withdraw function failed to validate that the LP token provided matched the pool's authorized mint address. This let an attacker mint a fake LP token and withdraw the entire pool's assets, a vulnerability in on-chain legacy code left callable with real funds.

name: Asterix
label: Access Control; Token Approval Abuse
rootCause:
Asterix, an NFT liquidity protocol forked from Flooring Protocol, was exploited on Ethereum Mainnet on 9 June 2026, resulting in a loss of approximately $40,000. The incident leveraged a vulnerability inherited from DN404/BT404-style token approval and accounting logic, allowing repeated unauthorized withdrawals from the pool.

A flawed token approval and accounting mechanism inherited from DN404/BT404-style logic enabled repeated illicit claims on pool assets, allowing attackers to drain funds via forged or reused token IDs.

name: NovaBox
label: Logic Error; Incorrect Share Accounting
rootCause:
NovaBox on Ethereum Mainnet suffered a $107,000 loss on 9 June 2026, when an attacker exploited a flaw in the reward distribution logic using a flash loan and a constructor-based deposit. The improperly sequenced dividend snapshot allowed the attacker to withdraw inflated dividends, nearly emptying the pool.

The NovaBox contract took a dividend snapshot before updating the new depositor's balance, allowing attackers to collect unearned dividends by joining through a constructor contract and immediately withdrawing ETH. The flawed sequence enabled 'phantom' dividend allocations.

name: Token of Power
label: Governance Attack; Malicious Proposal
rootCause:
On 9 June 2026, Token of Power's Aragon DAO on Ethereum was exploited when an attacker bought a majority of TOP tokens, passed an atomic governance proposal to mint 10 billion TOP, and drained 944.2 WETH (~$1.58M) from a Balancer pool. Net liquidity provider loss was ~281 WETH (~$472K), after accounting for the attacker's buy-in capital.

The DAO was vulnerable due to three missing defenses: uncapped minting in TokenManager (a code defect), no governance execution timelock (configuration flaw), and buyable majority through token concentration in the liquidity pool. The critical exploit vector was the uncapped mint.

name: Flooring Protocol
label: Logic Error; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
Flooring Protocol on Ethereum Mainnet suffered a critical accounting flaw on 8 June 2026, exposing over $500,000 in pooled NFTs to potential loss. A bug enabled unlimited minting of fpToken shares, creating a risk of draining pool assets. Yuga Labs led a documented white-hat rescue, securing 68 high-value NFTs, now in custody pending contract repair. All incident specifics are derived from technical press coverage and project participant statements; no chain forensics or official postmortem is available.

An ownership verification and accounting logic flaw allowed unlimited minting of fpToken shares unbacked by actual NFTs. Underflow errors and ghost ownership states enabled attackers or responders to withdraw more assets than users deposited, compromising pool security.

name: Humanity Protocol
label: Phishing; Private Key Compromise; Multisig Failure; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
A single phishing email to a Humanity Protocol director led to the theft of seven high-privilege keys, allowing attackers to bypass multisig protections, seize ProxyAdmin control on Ethereum and BNB Chain, drain locked H tokens, and mint billions of new H tokens. The attack inflicted over $36M in losses, with the Ethereum deployment later frozen and the BNB Chain permanently compromised.

The root cause was operational key management failure: seven critical admin keys, including multiple Gnosis Safe signer keys for both chains, were stored on a single compromised device. Once attackers gained remote access via phishing, they collected the keys and executed upgrade and minting actions across both deployments.

name: Ambient Finance
label: Deposit Logic Flaw; Surplus Accounting Error
rootCause:
Ambient Finance's DEX contract on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited on June 7, 2026. An attacker manipulated native surplus accounting in its single-contract design, draining over 83 ETH (valued at ~$110,600) via a deposit logic flaw. The attack involved flash-loaned WETH, complex pools, and multi-protocol fund routing.

Ambient's monolithic smart contract design failed to correctly account for native asset surplus during deposit and pool operations. The vulnerability allowed an attacker to harvest more ETH than deposited by exploiting flawed deposit logic and grid-stepped pool interactions.

name: Syscoin Bridge
label: Bridge Exploit; Forged Proof
rootCause:
On June 7, 2026, Syscoin's bridge was exploited via a proof-validation flaw, allowing an attacker to mint 5 billion unauthorized SYS tokens, valued near $10 million. The team paused the bridge, recovered the funds, and burned the excess supply. The root cause was a parsing ambiguity between Syscoin Core and its NEVM relay leading to inconsistent asset interpretation.

A parsing ambiguity between Syscoin Core and the NEVM relay allowed a UTXO burn to be interpreted as a native SYS burn on one side and as a custom asset on the other. This mismatch let the bridge release SYS tokens without proper proof.

name: ATM
label: Custom transfer logic flaw; Auto-swap vulnerability; Distributed account farming
rootCause:
On 3 June 2026, ATM Token on BNB Chain was exploited via a flawed transfer mechanism. The attacker repeatedly triggered a swap of 20% of transferred ATM tokens during each sell, draining approximately $243,500 from the liquidity pool. The vulnerable auto-swap logic, combined with weak anti-whale controls, allowed the attacker to farm and drain ATM/USDT LP funds.

ATM Token’s custom _transfer function contained an auto-swap feature that sold 20% of every transfer via PancakeSwap. This logic could be repeatedly triggered during sell transactions, leaking contract-held tokens and fee proceeds. Weak per-address anti-whale and anti-bot controls failed to prevent farming with multiple new accounts, enabling the drain.

name: GPU.NET
label: Logic Error
rootCause:
DefiLlama lists GPU.NET as an Ethereum incident on 2026-06-03 with about $10,600 lost. The accessible record identifies it as a Protocol Logic event, but does not reveal the specific logic flaw, attacker, or transaction path.

Unknown from the available evidence. DefiLlama classifies GPU.NET as a Protocol Logic incident with technique Unknown, but the available public evidence does not identify the broken invariant, function, or transaction sequence that caused the loss.

name: Gnosis Pay
label: Input Validation; Signature Verification Flaw
rootCause:
On 1 June 2026, a critical logic flaw in the Zodiac Delay Module used by Gnosis Pay wallets on Gnosis Chain allowed attackers to bypass EIP-1271 signature verification, enabling unauthorized withdrawals. Approximately $1.5 million was drained from user accounts, with additional funds locked. Gnosis responded by restoring balances, patching the vulnerability, and expanding security measures.

The deployed Delay Module (Zodiac v3.4.0) failed to check whether ERC-1271 signature verification calls succeeded, trusting the return value from isValidSignature even when the call reverted. This enabled attacker contracts to forge valid approvals.

name: TesseraDAO
label: Unauthorized Mint; Privileged Role Compromise; Access Control
rootCause:
On June 1, 2026, TesseraDAO on BNB Chain was exploited when an attacker gained privileged minting access and minted 99 million TSR tokens, selling them for approximately $2.4 million and collapsing the token price by 99%. Funds were routed through Tornado Cash, and no official postmortem or recovery plan was released.

Compromised privileged mint authority enabled the attacker to mint 99 million TSR tokens without legitimate authorization. No effective supply cap, multi-party approval, or timelock protected the mint function.

name: TesseraDAO (TSR)
label: Unauthorized Mint Privilege; Privileged Key or Role Compromise; Potential Mint Logic Exposure
rootCause:
On June 1, 2026, TesseraDAO's TSR token on BNB Chain suffered a catastrophic exploit: an attacker gained control of privileged minting rights, issued 99 million unbacked TSR tokens, and immediately dumped them into liquidity pools. Approximately $2.4,$2.5 million in project assets were drained and laundered via Tornado Cash. No official recovery or project technical disclosure has been published as of this review.

The incident resulted from unauthorized access to privileged minting authority for TSR on BNB Chain. The attacker was able to mint new tokens without backing, either through compromised admin keys, operational lapses, or insufficient access control on the mint function. Public evidence points to a failure in key/role protection, not a contract logic bug.

name: Fluid Lending
label: Operational key compromise; Off-chain Merkle reward system
rootCause:
On 31 May 2026, Fluid Lending's off-chain Merkle reward distribution system on Ethereum was compromised when an attacker gained control of both proposer and approver keys. This enabled unauthorized claims of over $215,000 in FLUID, GHO, and cbBTC, which were rapidly swapped and laundered via Tornado Cash.

The attacker obtained both proposer and approver keys for Fluid's Merkle reward system, bypassing intended 2-key authorization and enabling fraudulent reward claims.

name: AFI Protocol
label: Logic Error
rootCause:
On May 30, 2026, AFI Protocol's afiUSD vault on Ethereum was exploited, resulting in a loss of about $480,000. The attacker drained stablecoin assets, converted DAI to ETH, and routed a substantial portion through Tornado Cash. Investigations are ongoing, but the precise exploit mechanism has not been publicly disclosed.

The specific vulnerability exploited remains unconfirmed. No public post-mortem or technical disclosure from AFI has detailed the root cause. Multiple high-severity vulnerabilities were reported to the team before the attack, but which issue enabled the exploit is not established.

name: Alephium Bridge
label: Bridge Exploit; Forged Proof
rootCause:
On 30 May 2026, the Alephium Bridge on Ethereum and BNB Chain was exploited via forged guardian-signed messages, resulting in a loss of approximately $815,000 in custody assets and 13.76 million unbacked wALPH minted. Most unbacked wALPH was burned on-chain shortly after, but the backed custody assets were not recovered.

The bridge's off-chain re-observation path failed to validate fabricated events to the same standard as the primary observation path. An attacker exploited this weakness by orchestrating node disruptions and crafting a fake Alephium contract event, causing legitimate guardians to sign cryptographically valid but unauthorized VAAs, which were then redeemed for real assets.

name: AROS
label: Spot Price Manipulation; Oracle Manipulation
rootCause:
AROS was exploited on BNB Chain on 30 May 2026, resulting in losses of approximately $295,000, with the attacker draining protocol assets via flash loans, contract calls, and signature-based withdrawals. The precise vulnerable operation is unconfirmed due to the absence of a published protocol-side postmortem.

The incident involved rapid asset extraction using flash loans, approvals, and signature-based functions. Most evidence suggests a price/oracle manipulation or privileged claim/withdrawal path, but the exact contract vulnerability remains unconfirmed by the protocol due to the lack of an official postmortem or technical disclosure.

name: Gravity Bridge
label: Cross-chain registry poisoning; Denom mapping corruption via permissionless deployERC20; Missing input validation
rootCause:
Gravity Bridge lost roughly $5.4M on May 30, 2026 due to cross-chain registry poisoning. An attacker exploited weak validation in the bridge’s token-denomination mapping process, allowing withdrawal of real Ethereum assets in exchange for worthless tokens minted for free on Osmosis.

The cross-chain registry update process accepted a maliciously crafted Cosmos 'denom' string without validation. The attacker embedded the real addresses of Ethereum custody tokens in fabricated denoms, and the validator attestation process wrote these as trusted mappings, allowing the attacker to withdraw real assets without depositing real value.

name: DxSale
label: Ownership Override; Privileged Functions; Liquidity Rug
rootCause:
DxSale’s legacy liquidity locker on BNB Chain was exploited on 28 May 2026, draining an estimated $7.3 million from more than 1,400 liquidity providers. The attacker gained contract ownership through a series of concealed transfers and then used privileged functions to bypass lock restrictions, enabling mass withdrawal of funds.

DxSale’s locker contract allowed ownership to be transferred without public notice or resistance, eventually granting an attacker admin privileges. Using owner-level access, the attacker invoked privileged functions (such as backdoor and fee-setting operations) to manipulate lock periods and fees, bypassing user-level timelocks and draining the locked funds. No immutable enforcement or multi-signature constraints were present.

name: ONTR
label: Access Control; Ownership Takeover; Hidden Balance Inflation
rootCause:
ONTR token on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited on May 28, 2026, due to a flawed onlyOwner modifier and hidden balance-inflation functions. The attacker was able to seize ownership, inflate token balances, and drain 49.48 WETH (approximately $98,300) from the ONTR/WETH liquidity pool.

A custom onlyOwner modifier treated a renounced owner (owner = address(0)) as a pass-all condition, enabling any address to assume ownership and call privileged functions. Obfuscated functions allowed direct balance inflation without adjusting totalSupply or emitting events.

name: Stake DAO
label: Deployer key compromise; LayerZero cross-chain peer hijack; Unbacked cross-chain mint
rootCause:
Stake DAO lost approximately $91,000 on Arbitrum One after a compromised deployer key allowed an attacker to fraudulently mint and swap 5.4 trillion vsdCRV tokens by hijacking cross-chain trust via LayerZero. The incident was contained within an hour, with user backing secured and a compensation plan launched.

The deployer EOA retained owner privileges on the vsdCRV token contract for over two years because the governance handover process was never completed. This allowed the attacker, who compromised the deployer's key, to hijack the contract’s cross-chain trust and mint unbacked tokens.

name: SUPERFORTUNE AI
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
SUPERFORTUNE AI's May 27, 2026 GUA treasury transfer was redirected during a multisig execution, with public reporting placing the loss at about $15.18 million. The available record points to a signing or authorization compromise, and the public chain label is inconsistent across sources.

Compromised multisig authorization during a treasury transfer, likely through a leaked signing key or altered signature. The exact intrusion path is not independently established in the available public evidence.

name: SKP
label: Malicious transfer-hook with sync() manipulation; Privileged whitelist address enabling exploit; AMM reserve mis-accounting
rootCause:
On May 26, 2026, SKP on BNB Chain suffered a $212,000 exploit driven by a malicious transfer-hook that forced AMM reserve sync during trades. The attacker drained nearly all USDT from the PancakeSwap pair by manipulating reserves mid-transaction.

The SKP token included a custom transfer-hook that conditionally called sync() on its PancakeSwap USDT pair during token transfers. This allowed the attacker to collapse the SKP reserve mid-swap, making USDT extraction possible. The hook was deliberately added in SKP's contract design, triggered via privileged whitelisting. The vulnerability was not a generic share-accounting flaw but a maliciously constructed backdoor with premeditated access control.

name: Bitmor
label: Token Approval Abuse; Access Control
rootCause:
Bitmor, a Bitcoin-focused DeFi protocol on Base, suffered an exploit on 25 May 2026. Attackers abused the DCA contract's access to active ERC-20 token approvals, draining about $6,000 from user wallets. No primary on-chain evidence or team disclosure is available; findings rely on consistent reports across several monitoring platforms.

The DCA contract was able to use persistent ERC-20 token approvals without enforcing adequate limits on who could invoke token transfers or under what conditions, allowing attackers to withdraw funds from any user who had previously granted an approval.

name: New Market Trading
label: Access Control
rootCause:
An attacker exploited New Market Trading's SquidRouterModule by forging payloads that impersonated authorized delegates, draining $3.8M from 88 Gnosis Safe wallets across Ethereum, Base, and Arbitrum in under 15 minutes.

A confused-deputy vulnerability in SquidRouterModule: the contract validated the delegate via a payload field without checking that msg.sender matched the delegate, so anyone could impersonate an approved delegate and drain Safes.

name: WUSD.fi/Glove
label: Sybil incentive abuse; Reward logic flaw
rootCause:
On May 25, 2026, the WUSD.fi protocol's GLOVE reward system on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited through a Sybil incentive abuse, enabling an attacker to repeatedly mint reward tokens and drain $200,000 in USDC and USDT from GLO liquidity pools.

The reward eligibility logic in WUSD.fi's GLOVE contract only tracked the current token balance for each address without a persistent participation record, allowing unlimited reward minting by rotating through fresh accounts.

name: StablR
label: Private Key Compromise; Unauthorized Minting; Multisig Governance Failure
rootCause:
On 2026-05-24, StablR’s Ethereum minting authority was reportedly compromised through a weak 1-of-3 multisig configuration. The attacker allegedly seized administrative control, minted millions of unbacked USDR and EURR tokens, and sold part of the supply into thin on-chain liquidity, causing severe depegs and forcing StablR to suspend minting and redemption.

Public reporting indicates that a single compromised signer in StablR’s 1-of-3 Ethereum minting multisig allowed the attacker to add a malicious owner, remove legitimate signers, and gain persistent control over stablecoin issuance. No smart contract arithmetic flaw has been publicly identified. StablR had not published a detailed technical postmortem in the reviewed sources.

name: Fractal Protocol
label: Stale price manipulation; Permissionless compute(); Retroactive yield arbitrage; Flash loan atomicity
rootCause:
Fractal Protocol's yield vault on Arbitrum was exploited in May 2026 when an attacker used flash loans and permissionless price advancement to drain $13.7K USDC, leveraging a stale token price and mispriced receipt token minting.

The root cause was a permissionless price accrual mechanism in the vault's compute() function, which allowed any user to arbitrarily advance the token price without actual yield reserve funding. This enabled atomic minting at a low price and instant redemption at an inflated price within one transaction, draining the vault's withdrawal buffer.

name: Polymarket
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
On May 22, 2026, Polymarket lost approximately $700,000 on Polygon due to a compromise of an internal, six-year-old wallet's private key. The attack drained operational funds but did not affect user balances or core contracts.

A stale internal Polymarket operational wallet's private key was compromised, enabling an attacker to withdraw POL and USDC.e in scripted batches. No core contract logic was exploited.

name: Mure
label: Input Validation; Signature Verification Flaw
rootCause:
The MureDistribution contract on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited on 21 May 2026, allowing an attacker to drain approximately 4.85 million QUEST tokens, worth about $11,700, from an externally approved wallet. The attacker circumvented signature verification by supplying an attacker-controlled contract as both the source and the verifier, exploiting the contract's reliance on user-supplied data for authorization.

The contract based signature verification and the authoritative signer identity on a user-supplied contract. This contract was only checked for a self-declared interface (via ERC-165) and not authenticated against any trusted registry. As a result, the attacker could supply a contract that self-approved any signature (ERC-1271), enabling unauthorized token transfers from users who had granted pre-existing allowances to the distributor.

name: MAP Protocol
label: Infinite Mint
rootCause:
MAP Protocol’s Butter Bridge V3.1 accepted a crafted retry-message path on Ethereum mainnet and minted 1,000,000,000,000,000 MAPO to an attacker-controlled address on 2026-05-20. Public records and secondary reporting also place the incident on BNB Chain, but only the Ethereum transaction is independently reproduced here.

The bridge-side retry path accepted an unbacked MAPO mint. Public analyses attribute the trigger to weak message validation in retryMessageIn, likely involving packed-field hashing over dynamic data, but the historical victim source was not independently available, so the exact line-level defect remains unverified.

name: RetoSwap
label: Forged arbitration message; Multisig creation flaw; Missing identity/sender validation
rootCause:
RetoSwap, a decentralized Monero exchange running a Haveno Protocol fork, was exploited for roughly 7,000 XMR (~$2.7 million) on 20 May 2026 when attackers used a forged arbitration message to gain control of multisig wallets and sweep victim funds.

The protocol accepted forged arbitration messages without verifying the sender's signature or identity, enabling attackers to impersonate the arbitrator, update the node address, and obtain control during multisig wallet creation.

name: Bankr
label: Session Key Compromised
rootCause:
Bankr was listed as an incident on Base for 2026-05-19, with the public record attributing about $170,000 in losses to a compromised session key.

The supported cause is a session key compromise. The available record does not identify how the key was exposed or whether the exposure came from the frontend, backend infrastructure, a browser session, or another trust boundary.

name: Echo Protocol
label: Private Key Compromise; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
On May 19, 2026, Echo Protocol's Monad deployment suffered an unauthorized minting incident when an attacker used a compromised admin key to create 1,000 unbacked eBTC, with a notional value of $76.7M. Rapid containment limited the actual stolen assets to about $816,000, extracted via collateralization, bridging, and laundering through Tornado Cash.

Echo Protocol's eBTC mint authority on Monad depended on a single admin key with no multisig or timelock, enabling the attacker who obtained that key to mint unbacked assets without collateral or rate limits. This operational weakness allowed straightforward circumvention of supply and collateral checks.

name: ElevateFi
label: Spot Price Manipulation; Oracle Manipulation; Flash loan
rootCause:
ElevateFi’s Polygon staking vault was exploited on May 19, 2026 via a single-block spot price manipulation, enabling an attacker to inflate $2.5 million in staking principal with only 713 EFI and to claim 6,256 EFI as rewards, resulting in a confirmed loss of approximately $16,000,$25,000.

The ElevateFi staking vault relied on the instantaneous spot price read from an on-chain Uniswap V2 EFI/DAI pair via getPriceUSD(), which allowed the attacker to manipulate the reserves and set the price in the very transaction used for staking. No TWAP, external oracle, or manipulation resistance was used, so a flash-loan attacker could transiently set prices and permanently import that value into staking and reward accounting.

name: HermesVault
label: LogicSig rekeying vulnerability; Withdrawal Logic Flaw
rootCause:
HermesVault was exploited on Algorand on May 19, 2026 due to a withdrawal verifier bug allowing bypass of zero-knowledge checks, resulting in a loss of approximately 261,000 ALGO (~$30,000). Most stolen funds were refunded and the protocol was retired after a patch to its underlying zk verifier logic.

A withdrawal LogicSig verifier allowed malicious rekeying, which bypassed zero-knowledge proof checks and permitted unauthorized withdrawals. The flaw was in the script’s guard logic, not the cryptographic zk circuit.

name: Verus-Ethereum Bridge
label: Type-validation failure in bridge import logic; Improper message verification; Cross-chain validation bug
rootCause:
On May 18, 2026, the Verus-Ethereum Bridge suffered a $11.4,11.7M exploit when the Ethereum-side contract failed to verify that a proven Verus export object was a valid payout instruction. The attacker used crafted supplemental export data to trigger unauthorized release of ETH, tBTC, and USDC. Roughly 75% of assets were returned after negotiations.

The Ethereum bridge contract proved that a Verus export object existed but did not validate its type. It accepted supplemental export objects,which are not intended for payout,and parsed them as legitimate, enabling unauthorized asset release.

name: MetaSea
label: Logic Error; Flash Loan Abuse
rootCause:
MetaSea's SEA round product on Arbitrum was drained on 2026-05-17 when a flash-loan-funded helper contract repeatedly opened and redeemed positions in the same transaction, extracting SEA from a shared distributor and netting 13,904.941068 USDT in the focal exploit.

The round contract let a caller open and redeem in the same transaction, then claim SEA from a shared distributor using accumulated rewards rather than a time-weighted, per-position entitlement.

name: SEA Token
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
SEA Token's MetaSea round protocol on Arbitrum was exploited in May 2026. The attacker used a flash loan to repeatedly open and immediately redeem positions, draining reward tokens from a flawed settlement adapter and selling them for profit. Approximately $153,000 in value was extracted.

The vulnerable settlement adapter allowed immediate redemption of positions that credited reward tokens (SEA) based on the distributor's current accumulated balance, not user-time-weighted participation. There was no block or time lock preventing atomic open and redeem. Distributor payouts were unthrottled, so a flash-loan-funded loop could sweep the entire pending pool.

name: Adshares
label: Bridge Exploit; Forged Proof
rootCause:
On 15 May 2026, the Adshares bridge on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited via forged native-chain transaction IDs, resulting in unauthorized minting of Wrapped ADS tokens worth over $628,000. The attacker sold most of these tokens for ETH and USDC before partial funds were reportedly returned.

The bridge contract failed to verify that submitted native-chain transaction IDs corresponded to legitimate deposits, allowing the attacker to mint unbacked tokens by fabricating transaction identifiers.

name: THORChain
label: Private Key Compromise; Cryptographic Validation Failure
rootCause:
THORChain disclosed that a newly churned validator drained approximately $10.7 million from a single Asgard vault on May 15, 2026 after exploiting a vulnerability in the network's GG20 threshold-signature infrastructure. Public technical analysis attributed the incident to missing Paillier proof validation that allegedly allowed gradual leakage of signing-share material during repeated ceremonies until the vault key could be reconstructed offline.

THORChain publicly confirmed that the incident involved a vulnerability in its GG20 Threshold Signature Scheme implementation, but stated that the investigation remained ongoing and withheld detailed technical specifics. Secondary technical reporting attributed the compromise to missing MOD/FAC Paillier modulus proof validation in THORChain's GG20 fork, which allegedly allowed a malicious validator to register malformed Paillier parameters and extract signing-share material across repeated ceremonies until the vault private key could be reconstructed offline.

name: ShapeShift FOX Colony
label: Access Control; Arbitrary External Call; Meta-Transaction Authorization Bypass
rootCause:
ShapeShift’s FOX Colony treasury contracts on Arbitrum were exploited on 2026-05-13 through a meta-transaction authorization flaw in Colony Network’s EtherRouter architecture. Public analyses report that the attacker used executeMetaTransaction to trigger an internally authorized self-call, replace the contract resolver with malicious routing logic, and drain roughly $132,700 in USDC and FOX tokens.

Public postmortems attribute the exploit to an authorization bypass created by the interaction between Colony Network’s executeMetaTransaction meta-transaction flow and the legacy DSAuth authorization model. The contract executed attacker-controlled calldata through address(this).call(...), and DSAuth treated calls originating from the contract itself as authorized. That allowed the attacker to invoke privileged functions including setResolver without the intended administrative permissions.

name: Transit Finance
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
Transit Finance was exploited on Tron in May 2026, losing ~$1.88 million when a deprecated bridge contract allowed attacker-controlled calldata to drain user-approved stablecoin balances. The vulnerability persisted for years due to unresolved on-chain approvals.

A deprecated TransitMixSwapBridge contract allowed arbitrary calldata execution, enabling attackers to drain funds from users with lingering unlimited approvals. The lack of pause, self-destruct, or explicit approval revocation meant the legacy contract remained callable, exposing a persistent attack surface.

name: Aurellion Labs
label: Access Control; Uninitialized Proxy
rootCause:
Aurellion Labs lost 456,442.536622 USDC on Arbitrum One after an attacker reinitialized its Diamond proxy and drained preapproved wallets.

An initialize(address) path in the SafeOwnable facet remained callable because the proxy's _initialized version slot was never set, which let the attacker reinitialize the diamond and take ownership of the upgrade path.

name: BoostHook
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
On May 12, 2026, BoostHook's Uniswap V4 leveraged-long hook on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited for approximately $187,000. The attacker manipulated spot price to mint overleveraged positions, exploited a liquidation cap, and exited with 20.93 WETH profit, leaving the protocol with significant bad debt.

The BoostHook contract relied on manipulable spot pool prices to open leveraged positions and capped same-block liquidations at five, allowing attackers to create toxic debt positions faster than the protocol could liquidate them.

name: IEXCBP
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
DefiLlama catalogued an incident affecting IEXCBP on BNB Chain on 2026-05-12 with reported losses of about $97,000. The public evidence currently available for this entry is limited to a catalogue classification describing the event as spot price manipulation, and no primary exploit transactions, protocol disclosures, or vulnerable contract code were independently verified.

The only currently available public classification describes the incident as oracle manipulation through spot price manipulation. No independently verified exploit transaction, protocol disclosure, or vulnerable contract implementation was available to confirm the exact mechanism.

name: SQ Protocol
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
On BNB Chain, SQ Protocol's staking contract was exploited on 12 May 2026 for roughly $346,137 after an attacker used a hardcoded owner backdoor, forging staking positions and redeeming them for USDT. The attack drained both protocol and liquidity pair funds.

A privileged staking contract owner's access-control check included a hardcoded EOA exception, allowing the attacker to bypass ownership and execute admin-only mint, unlock, and token sweep operations.

name: Huma Finance V1
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control; Logic flaw in refreshAccount
rootCause:
On May 11, 2026, Huma Finance's deprecated V1 BaseCreditPool contracts on Polygon Mainnet were exploited via a logic flaw in access control, enabling an attacker to bypass credit approval and drain about $101,400 in USDC and USDC.e from three pools. The exploit was executed in a single orchestrated transaction, and the project’s V2 Solana contracts remained unaffected.

The refreshAccount() function in Huma Finance V1 BaseCreditPool allowed any caller to unconditionally promote a credit line to 'GoodStanding', bypassing the required Evaluation Agent approval check. This improper access control made unauthorized drawdowns possible.

name: INK Finance
label: Address-only claim authorization; Privilege escalation via contract deployment; Flashloan-assisted treasury drain
rootCause:
INK Finance’s Workspace Treasury on Polygon was exploited on 11 May 2026, draining around 140,180 USDT (approx. $140K) in a single transaction. The attacker bypassed identity checks by deploying a contract that passed a whitelist, enabling a treasury drain via a flashloan-funded claim.

The claimPayroll function failed to bind claimId to a stable, pre-authorized claimant identity. The contract only verified the caller address against a whitelist but did not check that the recipient matched a non-spoofable or immutable identity, enabling a newly deployed contract to trigger a treasury payout.

name: TAC Protocol
label: Bridge Exploit; Proof Verifier Bug
rootCause:
On August 22, 2026, TAC Protocol's Cosmos-EVM staking pool was drained of about 2.99 billion TAC tokens,28.6% of total supply,via an exploit targeting deficiencies in the shared EVM precompile module. The attacker sold roughly 1.26 billion TAC for around $1 million, with the rest still in attacker-controlled addresses. The vulnerability was in upstream code, and TAC halted its chain pending recovery and fixes.

Three combined defects in the Cosmos EVM module allowed integer underflow and incorrect copying of balances, enabling a protocol-controlled staking pool to be drained: (1) locked, unspendable tokens could be staked and deducted against the spendable balance; (2) the deduction had no lower bound, causing integer underflow; (3) the guard against manipulating protocol account balances did not apply to the affected path.

name: Renegade
label: Access Control; Uninitialized Proxy
rootCause:
Renegade's legacy V1 Arbitrum dark pool was exploited on May 10, 2026, due to an unprotected initializer in its proxy contract. An attacker drained about $209,000 across 26 ERC-20 tokens by injecting and executing malicious logic. Following on-chain negotiation, over 90% of the stolen funds (about $190,000) were returned to Renegade, leaving a net loss of around $19,000. User funds held in the affected proxy were impacted, but the protocol committed to full compensation.

A legacy proxy contract on Arbitrum was left with an unprotected initialize() function due to missing owner assignment and faulty migration. This allowed arbitrary external calls to instantiate attacker-controlled logic and perform privileged actions, including delegatecalling malicious code to drain held assets.

name: TrustedVolumes
label: Authorization Boundary Failure; Access Control; Broken Replay Protection
rootCause:
On May 7, 2026, the TrustedVolumes market maker lost about $5.87 million after an attacker exploited a custom RFQ proxy contract on Ethereum. The attacker combined flaws in signer authorization, access control, and replay protection to drain four major tokens from TrustedVolumes’ inventory wallet using their own contract as the exploit vector.

The RFQ proxy implemented an authorization boundary failure: it allowed any address to register arbitrary signers for itself, authorized signers relative to the taker (not the token source), and permitted token transfers from attacker-supplied addresses. The proxy also used broken replay protection, making the same signed order valid repeatedly within the same transaction. This combination let an attacker register their own signer, submit four forged orders referencing TrustedVolumes’ inventory, and drain the vault using its pre-granted unlimited approvals.

name: Ekubo
label: Access Control; Token Approval Abuse
rootCause:
Ekubo’s EVM-based swap router contract was exploited on Ethereum Mainnet on May 5, 2026. Attackers drained about 17 WBTC (~$1.4M) by abusing access to ERC-20 token approvals, allowing repeated unauthorized withdrawals from users who had granted allowances. The impacted functionality failed to check whether the withdrawal initiator was the rightful owner, targeting only EVM deployments and leaving liquidity-provider and Starknet users unaffected.

The Ekubo swap router’s payCallback and withdrawal logic lacked verification of the true payer or lock initiator. This allowed an attacker contract to repeatedly trigger token transfers from victim accounts with active ERC-20 approvals, bypassing proper access control and enabling multiple unauthorized WBTC withdrawals.

name: SmartCredit
label: Flash Loan Exploit; Protocol Logic
rootCause:
On May 4, 2026, SmartCredit's Leveraged Lido module was exploited on Ethereum Mainnet via a flash loan attack that drained approximately $72,000. The protocol paused the affected module and fully covered user losses using its Loss Provision Fund. No on-chain attack transaction or attacker address has been publicly disclosed.

Lending and accounting logic in the Leveraged Lido module failed to correctly enforce value and collateralization invariants under flash loan-induced rapid state changes, allowing temporary capital manipulations to extract protocol funds. The precise mechanism has not been made public.

name: SquidRouterModule
label: Improper Access Control
rootCause:
Attackers exploited the third-party SquidRouterModule installed in Safe (Gnosis Safe) wallets, stealing approximately $3.2 million from at least 86 accounts on Ethereum and Base. The module’s delegation relied on a hardcoded constant, allowing attacker impersonation and unauthorized withdrawals.

The SquidRouterModule's executeSameChainActions() function used a hardcoded constant string for delegate validation, allowing attackers to impersonate trusted delegates and bypass authorization in wallets with the module installed.

name: Bisq
label: Input Validation; Missing Input Validation
rootCause:
On May 1, 2026, Bisq v1 was exploited on Bitcoin, resulting in a loss of 11.59 BTC (roughly $550,000). The attacker used a modified client to supply a negative miner fee value, bypassing input validation and draining altcoin trade offers. Affected users were reimbursed through Bisq's DAO after emergency measures halted trading.

Bisq v1's trade protocol failed to validate taker-provided miner fee inputs. This allowed an attacker to pass a negative value, causing improper Bitcoin distribution in the multisig escrow output and redirecting excess funds to the attacker's change address.

name: Sharwa.Finance
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Sharwa.Finance on Arbitrum One was exploited on May 1, 2026, resulting in a loss of about $32,850. The attacker manipulated the spot price used to value Hegic option NFTs as collateral, allowing excessive borrowing followed by asset extraction.

Sharwa.Finance valued deposited Hegic option NFTs for margin trading using a spot Uniswap V3 Quoter, without resistance to immediate spot price manipulation. The attacker used ERC721 callbacks and flash loans to push USDC into a thin pool, manipulated the spot price, deposited the NFT as inflated collateral, and borrowed assets well above safe limits.

name: Wasabi Protocol
label: Private Key Compromise
rootCause:
On April 30, 2026, Wasabi Protocol lost about $5.7M after attackers compromised its deployer admin key, gaining unrestricted upgrade and withdrawal privileges across multiple EVM chains. The absence of multisig and timelock protections allowed rapid contract upgrades and draining of user vaults and protocol assets.

The Wasabi admin/deployer key (wasabideployer.eth), controlling privileged contract upgrades and withdrawals, was compromised. No multisig or timelock protected the admin role, enabling immediate UUPS proxy upgrades and funds drainage once a single key was breached. The exact infrastructure/key extraction path remains undisclosed.

name: Aftermath Finance
label: Logic Error; Input Validation
rootCause:
On April 29, 2026, Aftermath Finance's Sui-based perpetuals exchange lost roughly $1.14M USDC after an attacker exploited a signed/unsigned integer mismatch in its integrator fee validation logic, converting negative fee values into free collateral that could be withdrawn.

Aftermath Perpetuals failed to enforce non-negative bounds on integrator taker fee inputs and used a signed comparison on unsigned values. By setting a fee cap to zero and submitting a negative fee, an attacker passed validation and inflated their collateral through settlement arithmetic.

name: Sweat Foundation
label: Logic Error; Withdrawal Logic Flaw
rootCause:
SWEAT Foundation's NEAR token contract was reportedly exploited on 2026-04-29, draining about 13.71 billion SWEAT before the team paused the contract, froze liquidation channels, and restored external balances.

Reported refund-callback access control failure in the NEAR SWEAT token contract. The refund path was reachable outside the token contract's intended transfer-resolution flow, letting an attacker force refunds from victim balances. The exact historical revision remains unverified in the fetched record.

name: Syndicate Commons Bridge
label: Privileged contract role abuse; Malicious upgrade of bridge proxy; Single-signer key compromise
rootCause:
On 29 April 2026, the Syndicate Commons bridge on Base suffered a targeted protocol governance attack. The attacker seized upgrade admin rights, deployed malicious code to the bridge proxy, and drained 18.45 million SYND tokens (approx. $330,000,$380,000). Syndicate made all users whole using treasury reserves.

Excessive privilege of the UpgradeExecutor contract allowed an authorized executor to seize ProxyAdmin ownership, enabling a malicious bridge upgrade and draining of all funds. The exploit was enabled by weak upgrade key controls (single signer, no hardware/MFA, inadequate operational security).

name: JUDAO
label: Arithmetic Error; Logic Error
rootCause:
JUDAO's T3 token on BNB Chain was exploited on April 28, 2026, through a flawed ERC-20 sell-transfer hook. The attacker manipulated PancakeSwap pair reserves to withdraw 205,259 USDT and 36 BNB (~$227.9K) from the liquidity pool. The exploit abused tokenomics logic that debited pair tokens and updated reserves mid-transfer, breaking AMM accounting assumptions.

JUDAO's sell-transfer hook performed reserve manipulations and sync() calls inside the transfer logic, causing a mismatch between actual token balances and stored reserves. The vulnerable implementation allowed the attacker to create excess sellable reserves and extract more USDT than permitted by normal swap pricing.

name: Quant
label: Access Control; Arbitrary External Call; EIP-7702 Admin Delegation Abuse
rootCause:
Quant’s Ethereum reserve pool was exploited on 28 April 2026 due to a failure in access control. An externally owned admin account was routed through a public batch-execution path, allowing an attacker to drain 1,974.5 QNT tokens (about $138,000) in a single transaction.

The QNT reserve pool’s administrative authority was delegated to an externally owned account (EOA). This EOA could be targeted via a public batch-routing mechanism that lacked an effective access control boundary, allowing arbitrary external calls by anyone able to trigger the batch route. As a result, an attacker executed a privileged withdrawal and drained almost all pooled QNT tokens.

name: YieldCore
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
YieldCore's RWAVault on Ethereum was exploited on April 28, 2026, due to missing authorization checks in its ERC4626 withdraw and redeem functions. This allowed an attacker to withdraw matured principal from other users, draining approximately 392,764 USDC and causing a total vault outflow of 398,655 USDC.

YieldCore's RWAVault contract overrode ERC4626 withdraw and redeem, omitting ownership and allowance checks. Any caller could withdraw matured assets from any owner, bypassing the normal ERC4626 requirement that msg.sender be the owner or a valid operator.

name: Singularity Finance
label: Oracle Misconfiguration; Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Singularity_Fi's dynBaseUSDCv3 vault on Base was exploited on April 27, 2026, for approximately $413,000. An oracle misconfiguration allowed the attacker to mint nearly all vault shares cheaply, then redeem them against actual reserves, draining the protocol.

The vault's Uniswap V3 oracle was configured with an invalid fee tier (42), causing price queries for yield-token reserves to always return zero. This under-reported total assets, enabling the attacker to mint inflated shares and redeem them for nearly all real vault assets.

name: ZetaChain
label: Access Control; Token Approval Abuse
rootCause:
On April 26,27, 2026, ZetaChain was exploited through unauthenticated cross-chain calls and outstanding unlimited token approvals, resulting in a ~$333,625 loss from internal team wallets across four chains. No user funds were affected.

The GatewayZEVM contract allowed any external account to trigger protocol-signed arbitrary execution on GatewayEVM. Combined with existing unlimited ERC-20 token allowances from team wallets, this enabled attackers to drain funds through transferFrom calls.

name: Scallop Lend
label: Reward Logic Flaw; Cross-pool index manipulation
rootCause:
Scallop Lend was exploited on Sui on 26 April 2026, losing approximately $142,000 due to a reward logic bug in a deprecated auxiliary contract. The attacker manipulated a missing validation in the reward accumulator, allowing extraction of the full reward pool. Response actions contained further losses and protected user funds.

A missing validation check in the deprecated sSUI Spool contract allowed the attacker to pair unrelated reward pools and accounts, fabricating trillions of reward points and draining the rewards pool in a single transaction.

name: Litecoin
label: Missing MWEB input revalidation; Consensus patch coordination gap; Node DoS via mutated block
rootCause:
In March and April 2026, Litecoin's Mimblewimble Extension Block (MWEB) validation bug enabled fraudulent LTC creation and triggered a rare chain reorganization. The inflation event was fully contained on Litecoin and all tainted funds were recovered, but several cross-chain protocols,most notably NEAR Intents,credited swaps from the invalid branch, resulting in unreconciled exposures of up to 11,000 LTC. No end-user loss occurred on Litecoin itself, but third-party losses remain under review.

The block connection logic in Litecoin's MWEB implementation failed to enforce full input metadata validation, allowing miners to construct blocks with mismatched metadata and inflate peg-outs. Emergency fixes and node upgrades patched this issue. A separate DoS-triggered node coordination bug led to the April invalid branch and third-party exposures.

name: Purrlend
label: Access Control; Caller Impersonation
rootCause:
Purrlend paused its HyperEVM and MegaETH lending deployments on 2026-04-25 after an attacker used privileged bridge permissions to mint unbacked collateral tokens and borrow approximately $1.5 million in real assets. Public reporting attributes the incident to a compromised 2-of-3 administrator multisig that granted BRIDGE_ROLE access to an attacker-controlled address.

Public reporting attributes the incident to compromise of Purrlend's 2-of-3 administrator multisig. The multisig reportedly granted BRIDGE_ROLE privileges to an attacker-controlled address without a timelock or secondary validation, allowing the attacker to call a bridge minting function that created unbacked pUSDm and pUSDC tokens which were then used as collateral to drain lending pools on HyperEVM and MegaETH.

name: GiddyVaultV3 Ethereum incident
label: Incomplete Signature Coverage; Input Validation; Logic Error; Signature Abuse
rootCause:
GiddyVaultV3 was exploited on Ethereum mainnet on April 23, 2026, for approximately $1.3M. The attacker replayed valid EIP-712 signatures with modified SwapInfo parameters, abusing incomplete signature coverage to drain vault assets via malicious aggregator contracts.

Incomplete EIP-712 signature coverage in VaultAuth. Critical SwapInfo fields (aggregator, fromToken, toToken, amount) were not included in the signed struct, allowing an attacker to substitute them and drain vault funds using a reused signature.

name: Kipseli
label: Input Validation; Pricing/Decimals Mismatch
rootCause:
Kipseli's PropAMM router on Base was exploited on April 22, 2026. The attacker swapped 0.04 WETH for approximately 0.93 cbBTC, exploiting a pricing logic flaw that used a USDC-denominated quote as a cbBTC transfer. The loss, reported around $72,350, resulted from missing input validation and decimal mismatch.

The PropAMM router failed to verify that the quoted token matched the swap's output token. It used a USDC-scale quote when sending cbBTC, allowing the attacker to receive much more cbBTC than intended.

name: Volo Vault
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
On April 21, 2026, Volo Vault on Sui lost $3.5 million across WBTC, XAUm, and USDC vaults after an attacker gained access to the protocol's single-signature admin key through social engineering. No contract logic flaw was involved; asset freezes partially limited further loss.

A single admin private key, exposed via social engineering, allowed the attacker privileged access to directly drain three vaults. The design lacked multi-party authorization or separation of critical privileges, making one compromised operator a single point of failure. No smart-contract bug was exploited.

name: Juicebox V3
label: Input Validation; Logic Error; Missing Input Validation
rootCause:
Juicebox V3's REVLoans extension on Ethereum was exploited on April 20, 2026. The attacker drained approximately $52,000 in ETH by injecting fake loan sources with excessive decimals, manipulating protocol accounting to artificially inflate borrowable amounts and withdraw funds. Exploit and withdrawal transactions are now independently established.

REVLoans.borrowFrom() accepted arbitrary loan source terminal/token pairs without validating protocol registration or normalizing decimals. The attacker deployed a fake terminal reporting 36 decimal ETH context, seeded fake debt, and exploited mis-scaled accounting to borrow almost the entire pool.

name: Thetanuts Finance
label: First Depositor Attack; Logic Error
rootCause:
On April 20, 2026, Thetanuts Finance's BTC/USD vault on Ethereum Mainnet was drained via a share rounding vulnerability, resulting in approximately 0.15 WBTC loss (~$50,000). The exploit exploited faulty zero-supply share minting, allowing the attacker to withdraw pre-existing vault collateral.

The vault's share-minting logic failed to handle deposits when total supply was zero. This allowed the first depositor to set an overly favorable share rate, enabling later withdrawals to drain the vault's pre-existing collateral.

name: Transit Finance
label: Unknown
rootCause:
Transit Finance recorded a reported $257,800 exploit on Ethereum on 2026-04-20. Public evidence for this specific incident remains limited to exploit catalogues and monitoring dashboards, and no verified exploit transaction, vulnerable contract, or technical postmortem describing the attack mechanism has been identified.

Unknown. Public exploit catalogues list the April 2026 Ethereum incident under a protocol-logic classification, but no primary disclosure, verified exploit transaction, vulnerable contract, or technical analysis establishing the failure mechanism was located.

name: Custom sAVAX Rebalancer
label: Access Control; Arbitrary External Call
rootCause:
On 19 April 2026, the Custom sAVAX Rebalancer contract on Avalanche was exploited through an arbitrary external call vulnerability while holding Aave V3 credit delegation. Approximately 7,000 WAVAX (~$64,000) was borrowed against a victim but a whitehat bot frontran and recovered the funds before any malicious withdrawal, leaving no net user loss.

The Custom sAVAX Rebalancer contract exposed an unauthenticated external call interface, allowing anyone to execute arbitrary target calls,including Aave borrow actions,while holding unlimited credit delegation from victims. No access control or calldata validation prevented borrowing on behalf of other users.

name: Kelp DAO
label: Bridge Exploit; Cross-Chain Message Spoofing
rootCause:
Kelp DAO's rsETH bridge lost 116,500 rsETH, about $292 million, after a forged LayerZero packet passed a single-DVN path; Arbitrum later froze 30,766 ETH linked to the exploit.

A forged LayerZero packet cleared Kelp's Unichain to Ethereum route because the bridge trusted a single required DVN, and LayerZero's verification pipeline had been compromised upstream. Public reporting still disagrees on whether the 1-of-1 setup was Kelp's deployment choice or LayerZero's default configuration.

name: KelpDAO
label: Bridge Exploit; RPC Infrastructure Compromise
rootCause:
On April 18, 2026, KelpDAO's rsETH bridge lost approximately $292M after an attacker compromised off-chain RPC infrastructure supporting its LayerZero single-verifier configuration. The forged message led to a release of real rsETH on Ethereum, triggering cross-chain market freezes and partial recovery actions.

The exploit occurred because KelpDAO's rsETH LayerZero bridge was configured with only one Decentralized Verifier Network (DVN) , LayerZero Labs as sole verifier. The attacker compromised the DVN's downstream RPC nodes, forcing it to attest to a fabricated cross-chain message and release 116,500 rsETH without a corresponding event on the source chain.

name: Rhea Finance
label: Business logic flaw; Slippage calculation bypass
rootCause:
On April 16, 2026, Rhea Finance's margin trading on NEAR suffered an $18.4M protocol loss after an attacker manipulated slippage checks in swap routing. The attacker used fake pools to inflate the minimum output in leveraged trades, forcing undercollateralized positions that drained protocol reserves before being liquidated. Roughly $18M was later voluntarily returned or frozen; Rhea committed to covering the remaining shortfall.

The protocol's slippage check for margin position swaps summed min_amount_out values across all swap steps, counting amounts even when the output of one step was fully consumed in the input of the next. This allowed routes involving attacker-controlled tokens to artificially inflate the total minimum output without delivering real assets back to the protocol.

name: Grinex
label: Hot Wallet Key Compromise; Simultaneous signing authority
rootCause:
Grinex, a Russia-linked, Kyrgyzstan-incorporated exchange, suffered a coordinated hot wallet key compromise on April 15,16, 2026. Roughly $13.74M to $15M in USDT was drained from dozens of operational wallets across Tron and Ethereum, swapped into TRX within minutes, and consolidated at a single Tron address. No funds were recovered. Attribution claims of Western state sponsorship remain unsupported.

Simultaneous signing authority over multiple hot wallets was compromised, allowing an attacker to rapidly drain funds across two chains. The precise entry vector is unverified, but forensic evidence supports loss via operational key compromise rather than a contract bug.

name: CoW Swap
label: Frontend Compromise; DNS Hijack
rootCause:
CoW Swap's frontend was compromised by a DNS hijack on April 14, 2026, allowing attackers to redirect users to a phishing site and steal an estimated $1.2 million. The protocol's smart contracts remained unaffected, but users' wallet approvals were exploited through deceptive interface prompts.

Attackers used forged identity documents and social engineering to gain registrar-level control of the cow.fi domain, redirecting CoW Swap users to a pixel-perfect malicious frontend. This enabled wallet drainer scripts to extract assets by convincing users to sign broad approvals.

name: Zerion Wallet
label: Phishing; Social Engineering
rootCause:
Zerion disclosed that a company employee was compromised in an AI-assisted social engineering campaign on 2026-04-14, leading to the theft of about $100,000 from internal hot wallets. Public reporting indicates that user funds and Zerion’s self-custodial wallet infrastructure were not affected.

Public reporting and Zerion statements describe an employee-targeted social engineering and phishing campaign that exposed active sessions, credentials, and private keys for internal hot wallets. No smart contract vulnerability or wallet protocol flaw has been publicly identified.

name: Dango
label: Input Validation; Missing Input Validation
rootCause:
Dango suffered an exploit on April 13, 2026, when its insurance fund donation logic failed to validate positive input amounts. This allowed an attacker to drain about $1.9 million USDC from the perps contract, though bridge controls limited losses and all funds were ultimately returned after negotiations.

The insurance fund donation contract did not check that donation amounts were positive. Accepting negative values enabled an attacker to drain USDC collateral from the perps contract.

name: Hyperbridge
label: Forged Proof; Cross-chain Replay; Admin takeover and mass mint
rootCause:
On April 13, 2026, Hyperbridge’s cross-chain bridge contracts on Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain, and Arbitrum were exploited. An attacker bypassed a Merkle Mountain Range proof verification, forged a state proof, gained admin control, and minted nearly 1 billion unbacked bridged tokens, draining ~$2.5 million in liquidity across chains.

A missing bounds check in the MMR proof verifier (HandlerV1 contract) allowed forged proofs to pass and messages to execute. The flawed verification did not bind proofs to requests or check that all leaves were consumed, enabling replay and forgery attacks that granted admin and mint roles to the attacker.

name: MONA
label: Logic Error; Incorrect Share Accounting
rootCause:
On April 14, 2026, MONA was exploited on BNB Chain when a flawed deferred burn mechanism allowed an attacker to drain the MONA/USDT liquidity pool, resulting in approximately $60,950 in USDT lost. The exploit relied on delayed LP-token burning that could be triggered at attacker-chosen timing after the reserves had been manipulated.

The MONA token’s burn mechanism allowed tokens to be removed from the liquidity pool (LP) through a separate burn step, decoupled from the initial sell. The burn could be triggered via an ordinary token transfer (even zero-value), after the attacker had manipulated pool reserves, breaking the AMM’s pricing relationship and enabling the attacker to drain USDT from the pool.

name: SubQuery Network
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
SubQuery Network on Base suffered an access control exploit on 12 April 2026, allowing an attacker to drain over 218 million SQT from the Staking contract by replacing two privileged protocol roles, resulting in losses of approximately $131,000.

The Settings contract had externally accessible setBatchAddress and setContractAddress functions without any owner or role checks, allowing arbitrary mutation of critical protocol role addresses and enabling unauthorized withdrawal of staking funds.

name: Aethir
label: Access Control; Bridge Exploit; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
Aethir's cross-chain bridge adapter contract on BNB Chain was exploited on 9 April 2026. An attacker took contract ownership by calling an unprotected transferOwnership function, then drained approximately 423,000 ATH tokens (~$400,000). Funds were bridged to TRON, but prompt response limited user losses to under $90,000 with full compensation promised.

The AethirOFTAdapter contract's transferOwnership function lacked proper access control (such as an onlyOwner check), allowing any user to seize ownership and withdraw ATH tokens.

name: SquidMulticall
label: Improper Access Control; Permissionless Arbitrary Call
rootCause:
On April 7, 2026, an attacker exploited a SquidMulticall contract deployed on Arbitrum One, BNB Chain, Avalanche, Optimism, and Base, draining approximately $517,000. The exploit was enabled by users mistakenly granting token allowances to a permissionless arbitrary-call executor with insufficient access control.

The SquidMulticall contract's run() function permitted arbitrary external calls from any sender, lacking restrictions on caller identity, call target, or token spend source. Once a user approved the contract for unlimited token spending, any third party could drain those tokens by crafting transferFrom calls. A specific victim mistakenly approved SquidMulticall (rather than the intended router), which was immediately exploited by a bot.

name: Denaria Finance
label: Oracle Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation; Virtual AMM Manipulation; Rounding Error; Unsafe Cast
rootCause:
Denaria Finance was exploited on Linea on 2026-04-05, with public records putting the drain at about $165,618. Denaria later reported refunds totaling 6,319.062770 USDC to 60 addresses tied to Vault collateral and open positions, so the final unrecovered loss is not fully public. The published technical record points to a liquidity-accounting flaw in the LP settlement path, where rounding asymmetry and an unchecked signed to unsigned conversion turned corrupted balance state into withdrawable USDC.

Denaria's LP settlement path let a reconstructed balance component drift slightly below zero because of asymmetric rounding, then converted that signed value to uint256 without a non-negative check. The wrapped value was later capped to pool liquidity and treated as a valid collateral claim. A separate published analysis reconstructs the same incident as virtual AMM state manipulation feeding realizePnL(), but the incident-time source revision is not available here to reconcile the exact deployed path.

name: BSC TMM/USDT
label: Reserve Manipulation; Oracle Manipulation; Flash Loan
rootCause:
On 4 April 2026, the BSC TMM/USDT liquidity pool on BNB Chain was exploited via flash loan-driven reserve manipulation. The attacker burned TMM tokens to a dead address, desynchronized pool reserves, and extracted $1.665M USDT at a skewed price.

The pool contract failed to synchronize reserve balances after TMM tokens were burned, allowing attackers to manipulate spot pricing and drain USDT through a flash loan and swap sequence.

name: Drift Protocol $285M Multisig
label: Bridge Exploit; Signature Abuse
rootCause:
Drift Protocol on Solana suffered a $285M loss in April 2026 when an attacker exploited multisig governance using durable nonce accounts and social engineering. The attacker gained admin rights via pre-signed, delayed-execution transactions and drained vaults in minutes by fabricating a collateral market with a worthless token.

The incident resulted from a breakdown in Drift Protocol's multisig approval process. Social engineering led two Security Council members to pre-sign administrative durable nonce transactions. The attacker exploited Solana's durable nonce feature to delay and coordinate execution, bypassing timelocks and signer oversight. This gave them admin access and enabled them to whitelist worthless collateral, manipulate oracles, and extract real funds.

name: Silo V2
label: Oracle Misconfiguration; Protocol Logic Flaw; Supply Cap Bypass; Asset Accounting Error
rootCause:
On April 3, 2026, Silo V2’s soUSDC managed vault on Arbitrum was exploited due to a misconfigured oracle and protocol logic flaws, resulting in about $392,000 in losses. The attack focused on a peripheral meta-vault, with stale or preset price data combined with errors in accounting and cap logic.

A peripheral managed vault in Silo V2 on Arbitrum relied on an immutable, hardcoded oracle price for wstUSR, causing severe overvaluation of collateral after the asset depegged. This, together with protocol logic flaws in supply cap enforcement and asset accounting, allowed the attacker to extract excess funds.

name: Drift Protocol
label: Multisig governance compromise; Durable nonce exploitation; Fake collateral listing; Price manipulation
rootCause:
On April 1, 2026, Drift Protocol on Solana was compromised through a governance-layer attack. The attacker exploited durable nonce accounts and a low-threshold, zero-timelock multisig Security Council to pre-sign and execute administrative takeover, list fake collateral, manipulate oracles, and extract approximately $285 million through rapid protocol withdrawals.

The attacker used durable nonce transaction mechanics to keep pre-signed multisig admin approvals valid indefinitely, exploited a zero-timelock and low signature threshold, and socially engineered signers to bypass review. Lack of atomic state checks allowed listing and manipulation of fake collateral, resulting in massive rapid fund extraction.

name: Axios
label: Supply Chain Attack; Social Engineering; Malicious Dependency Injection
rootCause:
Malicious versions of the Axios npm package published on March 31, 2026, incorporated a hidden dependency that installed a remote access trojan on developer systems. Attackers gained access to sensitive credentials, posing risks for cryptocurrency operations and CI/CD pipelines until discovery and rapid removal.

A supply chain attack on the npm ecosystem enabled attackers to publish Axios package versions containing a malicious dependency (plain-crypto-js@4.2.1) that installed RAT malware. This was facilitated by compromised maintainer credentials following targeted social engineering and malware deployment.

name: LML/USDT staking protocol
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
On March 31, 2026, the LML/USDT staking protocol on BNB Chain was exploited for approximately $950,000. The attacker manipulated the LML/USDT price via flash-loan-driven trading, then immediately claimed and dumped inflated staking rewards. The exploit stemmed from a reward-claim path that settled using a same-block, attacker-controlled spot price.

The APower reward-claim entrypoint allowed rewards to be calculated and settled using a manipulable spot price fetched directly from the LML/USDT AMM. The attacker distorted the price in the same transaction as the reward claim, enabling over-withdrawal.

name: WhaleBit
label: Spot Price Manipulation; Oracle Manipulation
rootCause:
WhaleBit was exploited on Polygon Mainnet on March 31, 2026, via a same-transaction spot price oracle manipulation. The attacker moved the price of the CES/USDT0 pool, inflating redemptions and netting 10,506 CES (about $10,500). The manipulation succeeded because the protocol's price module relied on a live, manipulable spot price.

The WhaleBit staking protocol's deposit and withdrawal paths used the live spot price from the CES/USDT0 Algebra pool. This price could be manipulated within the same transaction by the attacker, allowing them to inflate the amount of CES redeemed after depressing the pool price. No TWAP (time-weighted average price) or tighter deviation guard prevented spot manipulation.

name: GoonFi
label: Swap Logic Flaw; Pool Mispricing; External Feed Error
rootCause:
On 28 March 2026, Solana-based GoonFi v2's WSOL/USDC AMM pool was drained of about $254,000 after an externally sourced price feed was accepted without sanity checks, enabling swaps at a grossly mispriced rate. Arbitrage searchers exploited this for rapid pool depletion. The affected program was halted immediately.

The GoonFi AMM accepted external price quotes with no bounds or continuity checks. A corrupted feed update set WSOL/USDC far below market, allowing profitable swaps at the erroneous price and draining all pool WSOL. The protocol lacked circuit breakers, minimum price enforcement, or pause logic to block severe mispricing.

name: Zoo Finance VTSwapHook
label: Price calculation bug (midpoint approximation); Reserve accounting error (pre-fee input credited); Chained swaps using callback flows
rootCause:
On March 28, 2026, the VTSwapHook contract on Arbitrum was exploited through a pricing and accounting flaw in its custom Uniswap v4 hook, allowing an attacker to drain the pool of approximately 2 million ATH and 4.5 million vATH. The exploit abused a midpoint price approximation and reserve inflation bug, resulting in substantial loss to liquidity providers.

The exploit arose from two compounding bugs in the VTSwapHook custom Uniswap v4 hook: (1) a midpoint approximation that systematically overestimated swap output on a nonlinear logarithmic curve, and (2) improper reserve updates that credited the pool's reserves with pre-fee gross input, inflating state and further distorting pricing.

name: TUR Staking
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
A BNB Chain staking contract branded as TUR Staking was exploited on 2026-03-26 after it calculated staking power from manipulable AMM spot prices. The attacker reportedly inflated the TUR price in TUR-NOBEL and NOBEL-USDT pools, staked during the manipulated window, and extracted amplified referral rewards worth about $133,000.

The staking contract derived staking power and referral rewards from live AMM reserve ratios read through spot pricing instead of a manipulation-resistant oracle or TWAP. Reported analysis also indicates the referral reward accounting granted additional reward power to referrer accounts without corresponding reward-debt adjustments, allowing attacker-controlled referral accounts to withdraw disproportionate TUR rewards after the price manipulation.

name: BCE
label: Logic Error; Incorrect Share Accounting
rootCause:
On 23 March 2026, the BCE token on BNB Chain was exploited for approximately $679,000. The attacker manipulated BCE's flawed burn mechanism, draining USDT from the PancakeSwap BCE/USDT pool by burning tokens from the pool's reserves, distorting the price and extracting value.

BCE relied on the scheduledDestruction variable to accumulate pending token burns, which were executed directly against the liquidity pool's balance instead of the seller's balance. This allowed attackers to manipulate pool reserves and pricing, draining stablecoins from the pool.

name: Cyrus Finance
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation; Flash Loan; Pool Share Accounting Manipulation
rootCause:
Cyrus Finance was exploited on BNB Chain in a flash-loan-enabled price manipulation targeting its PancakeSwap V3 LP-management logic. Losses were approximately $520,000, with attacker proceeds withdrawn as ETH and USDT.

The CyrusTreasury contract calculated withdrawal amounts by reading the current block's spot price from PancakeSwap V3's slot0, allowing a flash loan to manipulate the ETH/USDT pool price at withdrawal. Liquidity was removed disproportionately, favoring the attacker.

name: Resolv Labs
label: Compromised Off-Chain Key; Unchecked Minting (No On-Chain Validation); Access Control Failure
rootCause:
The Resolv Labs $25M exploit on March 22, 2026, was triggered by a compromise of an off-chain SERVICE_ROLE signing key. This enabled an attacker to mint 80 million unbacked USR stablecoins from minimal deposits, extracting around $25M before the protocol was paused.

A compromised off-chain SERVICE_ROLE private key enabled an attacker to call the Counter contract's completeSwap() function and mint arbitrary amounts of USR, unchecked by any on-chain mint cap, deposit validation, or multisig requirement.

name: Resolv USR
label: Frontend Compromise; Key Leaked via Infrastructure
rootCause:
Resolv USR suffered a major exploit on Ethereum Mainnet on 22 March 2026, when attackers gained signing authority over an off-chain key and minted nearly 80 million unbacked USR, extracting around $23.7M in ETH. The root cause was an infrastructure compromise, not an on-chain bug.

Attackers gained control over the protocol's SERVICE_ROLE signing key via a multi-stage infrastructure compromise, allowing them to call the USR Counter contract's completeSwap() function and mint unbacked USR. No independent on-chain mint cap tied to deposit value enforced limits.

name: Neutrl
label: Frontend Compromise; DNS Hijack
rootCause:
On 18 March 2026, Neutrl’s web frontend was compromised via DNS hijack, redirecting visitors to a fake site. Some users may have risked malicious approvals, but no direct protocol or user fund loss has been confirmed. Neutrl paused contracts, migrated to a new domain, and resumed safely.

Neutrl’s DNS records were hijacked, allowing attackers to redirect the project’s official domain to a malicious server presenting a phishing frontend. This put users interacting with the site at risk, but did not directly affect on-chain contracts or assets.

name: dTRINITY dLEND
label: Liquidity Index Manipulation; Flash Loan Accounting Bug
rootCause:
dTRINITY dLEND was exploited on Ethereum Mainnet on 17 March 2026 through liquidity index manipulation in its cbBTC lending market, enabling an attacker to borrow $257,000 in dUSD against phantom collateral created by flash loan premium dynamics. All bad debt was covered and the contract was paused.

A liquidity index inflation bug allowed an attacker to drastically increase the collateral value in the cbBTC reserve by setting totalLiquidity near zero and repeatedly applying flash loan premiums. The vulnerable index update formula lacked a minimum bound and sanity checks, enabling phantom collateral creation.

name: Fun.xyz CheckoutPool
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control; Calldata Binding
rootCause:
On 16 March 2026, the legacy CheckoutPool settlement contract on Polygon was exploited due to missing access control on its bridge() function. The attacker crafted a call that allowed funds held for settlement to be redirected to an attacker-owned smart account, resulting in a loss of approximately 85,730 USDC ($85,700).

The legacy CheckoutPool contract failed to restrict access to its bridge() function and did not validate that externally-supplied call data matched the intended checkout recipient. This meant anyone could route settlement funds via a crafted bridge call, allowing redirection to arbitrary addresses.

name: Venus Protocol
label: Supply cap bypass; Direct donation; Exchange rate manipulation
rootCause:
