The attacker created an illiquid DIGG,WETH pair, drained accumulated DIGG rewards for 81 ETH, and swapped them at favorable rates. This affected XSUSHI fee earnings but not user vaults.

SushiMaker relied on default swap bridges, with no custom bridge set for DIGG. DIGG fees accumulated and, when converted, were swapped through a user-created, illiquid DIGG,WETH pool. The absence of a bridge allowed outsized rewards to the attacker.

name: SushiSwap
label: Logic Error; Swap Logic Flaw
rootCause:
On January 25, 2021, a flaw in SushiSwap’s DIGG/WBTC pool fee routing logic on Ethereum allowed an attacker to harvest ~81.68 ETH in protocol fee revenue. Only protocol earnings were affected, not LP or user funds. The team restored correct routing by configuring a fee bridge for the pool.

Protocol fee conversion logic failed to set a custom bridge for new pools, causing SushiMaker to convert large accumulated DIGG fees via an attacker-created, illiquid DIGG/WETH pool. The attacker exploited outsized slippage by creating the missing pair and supplying minimal liquidity, capturing the protocol fees.

name: Saddle Finance
label: Unbalanced initial pool; economic arbitrage of mispriced AMM swap rates
rootCause:
Saddle Finance suffered a $275,000+ loss within an hour of its January 2021 launch on Ethereum due to unbalanced initial pool liquidity, allowing arbitrageurs to exploit pricing discrepancies and drain value from liquidity providers.

Saddle Finance launched stableswap pools without sufficient, balanced initial liquidity. This exposed the automated market maker to immediate price imbalances, enabling sophisticated arbitrageurs to obtain assets at mispriced rates and rapidly extract value from the pools.

name: Cover Protocol
label: Logic error; Solidity memory/storage bug; Infinite mint
rootCause:
On December 28, 2020, Cover Protocol suffered an infinite-mint exploit in its Blacksmith staking contract, enabling attackers to mint over 40 quintillion COVER tokens. Most of the proceeds were returned after the price collapsed, but the protocol and its users sustained significant losses.

A critical bug in the Blacksmith staking contract's reward accounting allowed memory state to be used instead of persistent storage. This enabled the attacker to repeatedly accrue and mint rewards based on outdated pool data, producing a nearly unlimited token supply.

name: LuBian
label: Key Compromise; Weak Key Generation
rootCause:
LuBian’s Bitcoin treasury was reportedly drained on 2020-12-28 after weak private-key generation exposed spend keys, with later analysis estimating 127,426 BTC lost and most of the coins still dormant.

Reported weak private-key generation in LuBian’s wallet setup, which may have made the relevant Bitcoin spend keys brute-forceable. The exact generator defect and the precise exploit path are not independently verified in the supplied primary evidence.

name: Altilly
label: Unauthorized admin account access; Backup deletion; Hot wallet loss
rootCause:
On December 26, 2020, Altilly, a centralized exchange, suffered a severe server and hot wallet compromise after attackers gained admin-level access to the hosting provider account lacking two-factor authentication. Backup deletion and wallet loss resulted in an unrecoverable loss of at least $750,000 and the platform's immediate shutdown.

The attacker exploited a hosting provider administrator account without two-factor authentication to gain full control over Altilly's infrastructure. This allowed administrative actions including server reboots, user creation, and backup deletion. While compromised API keys are reported as involved, primary evidence only supports broader admin panel control as the direct cause.

name: Livecoin
label: Infrastructure Compromise; Exchange Rate Manipulation
rootCause:
Livecoin, a Russian-based cryptocurrency exchange, suffered a catastrophic breach in December 2020. Attackers seized full control of the exchange's infrastructure, manipulated exchange rates, and facilitated mass withdrawals. The platform announced closure and an incomplete refund process after losses estimated at $3.3 million.

The attackers achieved administrative access over the entire Livecoin server and backend infrastructure, including custody and rate-setting mechanisms. This enabled them to rewrite core logic, manipulate asset prices, and drain funds. The precise vector of the initial compromise remains undisclosed by the exchange.

name: Exmo
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
Exmo's hot wallet keys were compromised on December 21, 2020, leading to unauthorized withdrawals of approximately $10.5 million across multiple cryptocurrencies. Deposits and withdrawals were rapidly suspended, security firms and exchanges were contacted, and affected users were reimbursed.

Hot wallet private key compromise enabled unauthorized withdrawals from exchange reserve accounts. The specific avenue of key extraction remains undisclosed in available sources.

name: Warp Finance
label: Flash Loan; Oracle Manipulation
rootCause:
Warp Finance was exploited on December 17,18, 2020, when an attacker manipulated the price oracle for Uniswap LP token collateral using flash loans. The attacker borrowed and withdrew roughly $7.7 million in stablecoins. The team later recovered a portion of the collateral, enabling reimbursement of about $5.85 million to users.

The protocol's price oracle for Uniswap LP token collateral relied solely on pool reserves, allowing an attacker to manipulate the LP price with flash-loans. The system did not use manipulation-resistant or time-weighted price references.

name: Nexus Mutual
label: Frontend Compromise; Key Leaked via Infrastructure
rootCause:
Nexus Mutual founder Hugh Karp’s Ethereum wallet was compromised on December 14, 2020, via targeted infrastructure and frontend manipulation. The attacker tricked Karp into signing a transaction, draining approximately $8 million in NXM tokens, which were quickly laundered through token wrapping, swaps, and cross-chain moves.

Remote access allowed an attacker to modify the browser's Metamask extension on the victim's machine, causing spoofed transactions to be signed with the victim's hardware wallet. The wallet signature was solicited for a transfer to the attacker’s address, exploiting both frontend control and personal infrastructure compromise.

name: Aeternity
label: 51% Attack; Majority Hashrate Attack; Double Spend
rootCause:
In December 2020, the Æternity proof of work network suffered a series of reported 51% attacks that targeted exchange deposits and attempted double spends. The publicly available record does not support the existing classification of a validator key compromise. Æternity stated that attackers temporarily controlled most network hash power, mined an alternative chain, and attempted to reverse exchange transactions involving roughly 29 million AE tokens.

The incident was a reported majority hash power attack against the Æternity proof of work chain. According to Æternity's public statements, attackers obtained more than 51% of network mining power, allowing them to mine competing chains and attempt exchange double spends. The available evidence does not support the previous classification of a validator key compromise.

name: Compounder Finance
label: Malicious contract upgrade; Admin drain; Insider rug pull
rootCause:
Compounder Finance was exploited in December 2020 on Ethereum when its anonymous admins used their upgrade privileges to replace secure contracts with malicious ones, draining over $12 million in user funds through insider-controlled withdrawals.

Compounder Finance's privileged administrators used the protocol's timelock-controlled upgrade mechanism to deploy malicious strategy contracts after audit completion, enabling backdoor withdrawals that drained user vaults.

name: SushiSwap
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
On November 30, 2020, SushiSwap was exploited on Ethereum Mainnet due to improper access control around its Sushibar fee-reward logic. An attacker was able to withdraw protocol fees, resulting in approximately $15,000 in losses, which were later covered by the SushiSwap treasury. No user funds or pool liquidity were lost and the exploit was patched within hours.

Lax access control in the Sushibar fee-rewards logic allowed an attacker to withdraw protocol fees by invoking reward-handling functions in an unintended sequence or manner not properly restricted to authorized actors.

name: Pickle Finance
label: Protocol Logic; Missing Access Control
rootCause:
On November 21, 2020, Pickle Finance was exploited for approximately $19.7M DAI due to missing Jar validation in its ControllerV4 contract. An attacker injected a fake Jar, bypassed checks in swapExactJarForJar, and withdrew assets from the cDAI Jar.

ControllerV4's swapExactJarForJar function failed to restrict Jar inputs to registered or whitelisted contracts. The attacker created a malicious contract with the expected interface, allowing unauthorized transfer of assets from the real cDAI Jar.

name: Origin Protocol
label: Reentrancy; Flash Loan
rootCause:
Origin Dollar (OUSD) was exploited for over $7 million on November 17, 2020, when a reentrancy vulnerability in its vault contract allowed an attacker to inflate their OUSD balance using a malicious token and a flash loan. The bug stemmed from a missing validation check that had been mistakenly removed during refactoring, leaving the contract exposed.

A validation check preventing reentrancy was accidentally removed from the OUSD vault contract during a refactor, enabling external ERC-20 token contracts to reenter the vault via callback before vault accounting was updated.

name: CheeseBank
label: Price Manipulation; Spot Price Manipulation
rootCause:
CheeseBank was exploited on Ethereum Mainnet on 6 November 2020 for approximately $3.3 million in USDC, USDT, and DAI. The attacker manipulated the spot price of CHEESE on UniswapV2 using a large flash loan, inflated collateral value, and borrowed the maximum from the protocol's lending pool before repaying the loan and withdrawing the stolen assets.

CheeseBank calculated UniswapV2 LP token collateral value using a spot price oracle derived directly from the WETH balance in the Uniswap pool. This value could be manipulated via flash loans, allowing an attacker to temporarily and massively inflate the LP price, deceive the protocol's collateral logic, and extract more assets than otherwise possible.

name: Value DeFi
label: Flash Loan
rootCause:
Value DeFi’s MultiStablesVault on Ethereum was exploited for approximately $6 million through a flash loan and oracle manipulation. The attacker used a flash loan to distort Curve stablecoin prices, allowing them to mint and redeem vault shares at artificially favorable rates in a single transaction. The vault’s price oracle trusted unreliable spot prices vulnerable to manipulation.

The vault minted shares based on conversion rates from Curve pool spot prices. Because the price oracle did not account for manipulation risk, a flash loan could temporarily distort these prices and result in over-minting of vault shares. The protocol’s oracle and deposit logic did not protect against single-transaction spot price manipulation.

name: Akropolis
label: Flash Loan; Reentrancy; Malicious ERC-20 Callback
rootCause:
On November 12, 2020, Akropolis's Ethereum savings pools were exploited for over 2 million DAI. The attacker used a flash loan and a custom ERC-20 token to trigger reentrancy in the pool's deposit function, manipulating pool share credits and draining funds.

The Akropolis savings pool deposit function violated the Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) pattern, calling external ERC-20 transferFrom before updating share and pool balances. This, combined with lack of reentrancy protection and an absence of token allowlist, let a malicious token re-enter deposit(), causing share inflation and draining funds.

name: Grin
label: 51% Attack; Majority Hashrate Attack
rootCause:
On 2020-11-08, the Grin network experienced a reported 51% attack after an unknown miner temporarily controlled most of the network hash rate. Public reporting and pool telemetry described chain reorganizations and elevated confirmation risk, but no verified loss amount or confirmed double-spend transaction was publicly documented.

Available reporting indicates the incident was a proof-of-work majority hash rate attack against the Grin network, not a confirmed validator key compromise. An unknown miner reportedly accumulated more than 50% of the network hash power, enabling block reorganizations and threatening transaction finality.

name: Ledger
label: Social Engineering; Phishing
rootCause:
Ledger users were targeted by phishing campaigns in November 2020 following a prior marketing data breach. At least $271,000 in assets were stolen after victims revealed their wallet recovery phrases to attackers via fake upgrade emails and websites.

Ledger's July 2020 marketing data breach enabled large-scale phishing campaigns. Attackers used exposed customer email addresses and personal information to craft convincing phishing emails, leading users to fake Ledger websites and prompting them to reveal their recovery phrases. This gave attackers full access to victims' crypto wallets.

name: Axion
label: Logic Error; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
Axion’s Ethereum launch was broken on 2020-11-02 by an infinite-mint exploit that minted 79.228 billion AXN, sold the tokens for 1,309.726383687296628968 ETH, and left a reported loss near $500,000.

A deployment-time code injection in the Axion staking contract’s OpenZeppelin AccessControl dependency let the unstake path mint AXN without a backing stake.

name: EtherCrash
label: Key Compromise; Cold Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
EtherCrash reported that its bankroll wallet on Ethereum Mainnet was compromised on 2020-10-26, with about 6,378 ETH, roughly $2.5 million, removed. The available record does not identify the exact compromise path or provide incident-time withdrawal hashes.

A wallet that controlled EtherCrash bankroll funds was compromised, allowing unauthorized withdrawals. The public record does not establish whether the access came from a stolen private key, insider action, or another operational failure.

name: Harvest Finance
label: Flash Loan; Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Harvest Finance was exploited on October 26, 2020 for approximately $24 million through repeated flash-loan-fueled manipulation of Curve’s spot prices, allowing the attacker to mint inflated vault share balances and instantly withdraw more stablecoins than initially deposited.

Harvest vaults calculated deposit and withdrawal amounts using manipulable Curve pool spot prices instead of a manipulation-resistant oracle. The contracts allowed attackers to inflate their fUSDC/fUSDT share allocations by temporarily depressing the underlying asset value, then withdraw at restored rates. Critical checks such as depositArbCheck() used overly permissive parameters and did not prevent the exploit.

name: LeoFinance
label: Private key compromise; Unrestricted contract minting
rootCause:
On October 11, 2020, an attacker used a compromised WLEO contract minting key to create unlimited tokens, draining $42,000 in ETH from the Uniswap liquidity pool. The breach stemmed from the use of a hot wallet private key with no minting limits or multisig. Rapid community action recovered some funds and prompted a refactor of WLEO architecture to remove arbitrary minting and strengthen key security.

The WLEO mint contract's private key, stored in a hot wallet with single-signer control, was compromised, granting the attacker unlimited mint authority. The design lacked minting limits, multi-signature protection, or supply controls, allowing arbitrary issuance and direct draining of the Uniswap pool.

name: WLEO
label: Key Compromise; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
On October 11, 2020, WLEO was exploited on Ethereum by an attacker who used the compromised contract key to mint unbacked tokens, extracting approximately $42,000 from the Uniswap liquidity pool. Rapid community response limited further loss, but the vulnerability allowed infinite minting.

The exploit was caused by key compromise. The attacker obtained the private key controlling the WLEO contract and used it to mint unbacked tokens, enabling infinite mint and draining assets from the liquidity pool.

name: Eminence
label: Flash Loan; Logic Error
rootCause:
On September 29, 2020, unreleased Eminence contracts on Ethereum were exploited, draining ~$15M from users who interacted with unaudited bonding-curve code. The attacker later returned $8M, and partial compensation was distributed, but $7M remains unrecovered.

The Eminence pre-production bonding-curve contracts allowed recursive mint-burn cycles that could be manipulated by flash-loan-funded transactions to extract more value than deposited. This logic error was deployed unaudited to mainnet, allowing public access and catastrophic fund loss.

name: KuCoin
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
KuCoin’s hot-wallet private keys were compromised in late September 2020, allowing unauthorized withdrawals across Bitcoin, Ethereum and several other networks. KuCoin later said it recovered or covered the affected assets through freezes, token swaps, judicial recovery and insurance.

Leak of KuCoin hot-wallet private keys. KuCoin said the attackers could withdraw from hot wallets after the compromise, but it did not publicly establish the exact exfiltration path.

name: Soda Protocol
label: Logic Error; Withdrawal Logic Flaw
rootCause:
Soda Protocol suffered an exploit on Ethereum Mainnet on September 20, 2020, due to a smart contract logic flaw in the withdrawal or liquidation mechanism. Attackers were able to liquidate user collateral illicitly, resulting in losses estimated around $160,000. The protocol team later patched the bug and partially compensated affected users with protocol tokens.

A critical flaw in the smart contract's liquidation or withdrawal logic allowed attackers to improperly liquidate over-collateralized loans, causing principal loss to user deposits.

name: bZx
label: Logic Error
rootCause:
On September 13, 2020, the bZx protocol suffered a major exploit on Ethereum when an attacker used a token self-transfer bug to duplicate iToken balances, draining about $8.1M in LINK, ETH, and stablecoins. The vulnerable transfer logic allowed repeated self-transfers to inflate iToken balances, which could then be redeemed for underlying assets. The protocol halted activity, patched the bug, and the attacker returned stolen funds.

The iToken contract's internal transfer logic failed to prevent self-transfers, which resulted in a net balance increase for the sender when tokens were transferred to the same account. This bug allowed attackers to repeatedly inflate their balance and redeem fake iTokens for real assets.

name: Coral Finance
label: Reentrancy
rootCause:
Coral Finance, a DeFi project on EOS, was exploited on September 10, 2020, resulting in the draining of over 120,000 EOS, valued at approximately $420,000. The attack was enabled by a reentrancy flaw likely involving wRAM handling, with no verifiable recovery or technical postmortem published.

A missing checks-effects-interactions pattern in Coral Finance's EOS smart contract allowed a reentrancy attack. The contract failed to update user balances before executing external calls, particularly involving wRAM transfers. This enabled repeated withdrawals and draining of the protocol's assets.

name: SYFI
label: Arithmetic Error; Logic Error
rootCause:
SYFI, an adaptive cryptocurrency on Ethereum, suffered a rebase arithmetic exploit on 2020-09-03, draining roughly $250K from its Uniswap pool when faulty logic allowed one trader to massively inflate and sell their token balance for ETH.

The SYFI rebase mechanism altered user balances without properly adjusting the Uniswap pool price, enabling an attacker to sell an inflated SYFI balance for ETH and drain most liquidity. Both arithmetic miscalculation and flawed sequencing enabled the exploit.

name: Eterbase
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
On September 8, 2020, Eterbase's hot wallets were compromised, resulting in the theft of over $5.3 million across six major chains. The breach led to immediate suspension of exchange operations and a prolonged operational disruption.

Attackers gained access to the private keys of Eterbase's hot wallets, enabling unauthorized withdrawal of assets across Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Tezos, Algorand and TRON. The lack of robust multi-signature or cold-storage controls allowed a single compromise to drain all hot wallet funds.

name: Soft Yearn
label: Logic Error
rootCause:
On September 3, 2020, Soft Yearn (SYFI) was exploited on Ethereum due to a faulty rebasing mechanism. The attacker turned a minor investment into over $250,000 by timing trades around a flawed supply adjustment in the SYFI token, draining the Uniswap liquidity pool.

Soft Yearn’s rebase logic failed to synchronize token supply expansions with Uniswap pool accounting. This allowed a holder to immediately sell an inflated balance after supply adjustment, extracting liquidity before pool pricing adapted. Accounting for LP balances and rebased supply was not robust.

name: OKEx
label: 51% attack; Chain reorganization; Double-spend
rootCause:
On August 18, 2020, OKEx lost approximately $5.6 million in Ethereum Classic due to a coordinated 51% attack, where an attacker reorganized the chain to double-spend coins after exchanging and withdrawing ZEC. All detailed evidence is drawn from OKEx disclosures and secondary media; no primary on-chain records or technical postmortem are published.

The attacker rented majority hash power on Ethereum Classic, secretly mined a shadow chain, and ultimately replaced the main ETC chain to invalidate their deposit to OKEx after withdrawing exchanged ZEC, enabling a double-spend. All evidence relies on OKEx's narrative and media summaries, as no direct forensic or chain proof is published.

name: Ethereum Classic
label: Bridge Exploit; Forged Proof
rootCause:
On August 6, 2020, Ethereum Classic suffered a second major 51% attack that resulted in a reorganization of 4,236 blocks and an estimated loss of $1.68 million (238,306 ETC) through successful double-spends. This exploit was enabled by rented hashpower, not a contract vulnerability.

The attacker controlled a majority of network hashpower and reorganized the chain to double-spend funds, exploiting Ethereum Classic's low Proof-of-Work security and absence of external checkpointing. No smart contract was directly vulnerable.

name: Opyn
label: Logic Error
rootCause:
On August 4, 2020, an exploit in Opyn's ETH put option contracts on Ethereum allowed an attacker to drain roughly $371,000 in USDC by abusing the exercise logic to double-spend oTokens in a single transaction. The protocol fully reimbursed affected put sellers and secured remaining funds via coordinated white-hat recovery.

The Opyn ETH put option contract allowed the exercise function to use the same msg.value for multiple internal exercise calls within a single transaction, enabling double spending of ETH put oTokens and USDC collateral when exercising against multiple vaults simultaneously.

name: 2gether
label: Custodial Platform Compromise
rootCause:
2gether reported the theft of 114 BTC and 281 ETH from investment accounts on July 31, 2020, together with password exposure. A later EUR 1.5 million funding round supported reported BTC/ETH compensation for 91% of affected users; the largest balances faced separate arrangements as the cost of replacing the coins rose.

Attackers gained access sufficient to remove assets from 2gether's investment-account environment. The company reported a server breach and password exposure but did not disclose the initial-access technique, credential permissions or withdrawal-signing path.

name: Cashaa
label: Operational workflow exception; Malware compromise; Key leak due to infrastructure
rootCause:
Cashaa's Bitcoin wallets were compromised in July 2020 when malware installed on an employee's personal computer enabled attackers to steal approximately 336 BTC. Operational security lapses allowed the attacker to access wallet credentials and transfer funds.

An employee used a personal computer for OTC wallet management after reporting a malfunction with the company device. Malware installed on this machine allowed attackers to retrieve wallet credentials and sign unauthorized transactions, bypassing normal security, with no multi-signature enforced.

name: Vether
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
Vether V3 suffered a major access control exploit on Ethereum Mainnet in late June 2020, when an attacker drained nearly all tokens from its contract, causing approximately $450,000 in losses and making the asset essentially worthless overnight. The protocol relaunched as Vether V4 and reimbursed affected holders.

The Vether V3 contract allowed an address exclusion from transfer fees but failed to properly restrict who could claim all tokens. The upgrade path bypassed standard ERC-20 permission checks, letting an attacker use the exclusion feature to seize nearly the entire supply. This improper access control exposed the funds.

name: Balancer
label: Flash Loan; Logic Error; Fee-on-Transfer Token Accounting
rootCause:
On June 28, 2020, an attacker exploited Balancer V1 pools on Ethereum that contained fee-on-transfer tokens including STA. Balancer tracked nominal token amounts in its internal accounting instead of the actual post-fee balances received by the pool. Repeated flash-loan-funded swaps and calls to gulp() drove the recorded STA balance near zero, allowing the attacker to drain WETH, WBTC, SNX, and LINK from affected pools.

Balancer V1 pool accounting assumed ERC-20 transfers delivered the full requested amount. Fee-on-transfer tokens such as STA burned 1% during transfers, causing the pool's internal _records balances to diverge from actual token balances. The attacker repeatedly amplified this mismatch through swaps and then called gulp() to synchronize the pool to the depleted real balance, creating an extreme price distortion that allowed other pool assets to be drained.

name: Bancor Protocol
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
Bancor V3 suffered a critical access control vulnerability on Ethereum mainnet in June 2020. Attackers and a Bancor white-hat team exploited a public safeTransferFrom function to drain user-approved tokens, resulting in losses and partial recovery. The exploit allowed arbitrary transfers from user wallets with unlimited approval.

The safeTransferFrom function was inappropriately declared public in the Bancor contract, allowing anyone to invoke it to transfer tokens from any user who had approved the contract. This enabled direct theft of user funds.

name: Hegic
label: Logic Error; Deposit Logic Flaw
rootCause:
Hegic’s April 2020 Ethereum incident left expired option liquidity locked in the pool contracts after a bug in the unlock path, with DefiLlama recording about $28,537 of impact.

A typo in the expired-option liquidity unlock path prevented collateral from being released after expiry, so the affected liquidity stayed locked in the pool contracts.

name: dForce Lending
label: ERC-777 callback reentrancy
rootCause:
On 19 April 2020, dForce Lendf.Me on Ethereum was drained of approximately $25 million across multiple assets due to a reentrancy vulnerability in its handling of the ERC-777 imBTC collateral. The attacker exploited the tokensReceived callback to inflate their collateral and borrow all pool assets. dForce identified the attacker via KYC, resulting in full fund recovery within two days.

Lendf.Me's supply and withdraw functions violated the Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) pattern when interacting with ERC-777 tokens like imBTC. The protocol transferred tokens before updating internal accounting, allowing an attacker to exploit the ERC-777 tokensReceived callback for reentrancy, repeatedly inflating collateral balances and borrowing all pool liquidity.

name: Uniswap V1 imBTC pool
label: ERC777 reentrancy; reserve pricing stale state
rootCause:
On April 18, 2020, Uniswap V1's imBTC-ETH pool on Ethereum was drained of approximately $220,000 due to an ERC777 reentrancy vulnerability. The attacker exploited Uniswap's swap logic and imBTC's callback hooks to manipulate reserve pricing, enabling extraction of extra ETH with repeated token-to-ETH swaps.

The Uniswap V1 contract priced ETH payouts based on the pool's current token balance, paid out ETH, and then only afterwards pulled tokens via transferFrom. Because ERC777 tokens (imBTC) allowed sender callbacks via tokensToSend before balances moved, the attacker could re-enter the swap function before the pool's reserves updated, letting both sells price against the same stale reserve and draining the pool.

name: Bisq
label: Protocol Logic; Withdrawal Logic Flaw
rootCause:
Bisq’s v1.2 protocol flaw allowed attackers to hijack fallback payouts during trade timeouts, resulting in thefts totaling approximately 3 BTC and 4,000 XMR (~$250,000) from seven users in April 2020. Trading was suspended and the flaw was promptly patched.

Bisq v1.2 did not verify that the fallback payout address matched the DAO-set donation address when resolving deadlocked trades. Attackers could set this address, redirecting funds from timeouts directly to their own wallet.

name: MakerDAO
label: Liquidation Auction Failure; Mempool Congestion; Zero-Bid Liquidations
rootCause:
During the March 12, 2020 Black Thursday market crash, MakerDAO liquidations on Ethereum executed under extreme network congestion. Keeper bots failed to submit competitive bids in collateral auctions, allowing zero-DAI bids to win large amounts of ETH collateral and leaving the protocol with millions in bad debt.

MakerDAO's liquidation design assumed that competing keeper bots would remain able to participate in collateral auctions during periods of market stress. On March 12, 2020, extreme Ethereum congestion and rapidly rising gas prices prevented many keepers from submitting or replacing bids in time. Auctions with minimal or no competition settled at near-zero or zero DAI bids, transferring collateral without adequately covering vault debt.

name: bZx
label: Flash Loan; Price-Impact Slippage/Position Health Validation Failure
rootCause:
On February 15, 2020, bZx's Fulcrum protocol suffered a flash-loan-powered exploit, causing a major loss of ETH after a leveraged margin trade was executed with a severely price-impacted swap. The protocol failed to enforce a post-slippage position health check, enabling the attacker to drain collateral and profit from arbitrage.

bZx's Fulcrum margin trading contract failed to validate position health after a high-slippage leveraged swap. A logic bug let the collateralization check be bypassed, allowing a severely undercollateralized position to be opened and exploited.

name: Ooki
label: Spot Price Manipulation; Oracle Manipulation
rootCause:
On February 15, 2020, Ooki (then bZx) was exploited on Ethereum mainnet. The attacker manipulated oracle price inputs via AMM swaps and multi-protocol flash loans, bypassing critical checks, which resulted in losses of approximately $650,000.

Ooki's price oracle accepted spot prices directly from multiple on-chain DEXes (Kyber/Uniswap), with no aggregation or deviation bounds. A logic flaw let an attacker bypass slippage checks for overcollateralized loans, enabling profit from manipulated collateral values.

name: Trinity Wallet
label: Frontend Compromise; CDN Compromise
rootCause:
On February 12, 2020, attackers exploited a third-party CDN dependency in the Trinity Wallet for IOTA, leading to the theft of approximately 8.55 Ti in IOTA tokens (valued near $2 million at the time). The compromised dependency enabled exfiltration of users’ seeds when the wallet was unlocked, allowing the attacker to transfer funds from affected wallets. The incident forced IOTA to halt its Coordinator and develop a seed migration plan.

The Trinity Wallet integrated MoonPay’s SDK via a CDN, without thoroughly mitigating the security risks of remote code loading. Attackers compromised MoonPay’s CDN, served malicious code to Trinity users, and exfiltrated user seeds when the wallet was unlocked, enabling theft of tokens.

name: Altsbit
label: Hot wallet compromise; Infrastructure exposure
rootCause:
Altsbit, a recently rebranded Italian exchange, was breached on February 5, 2020, losing $317,000 worth of BTC, ETH, ARRR, VRSC, and KMD held in hot wallets. About half of all user assets were stolen. Only cold wallet balances allowed partial refunds, and the platform ceased operations after the refund window ended. No technical vulnerability or forensic root cause was published.

Altsbit stored a majority of user assets in online hot wallets vulnerable to unauthorized access. The exact attack mechanism,whether leaked keys or compromised infrastructure,was not publicly disclosed. Key or infrastructure exposure is inferred from platform and industry reporting.

name: LuckLambo104
label: Transaction rollback attack; Protocol logic flaw
rootCause:
On 3 February 2020, the LuckLambo104 gaming DApp on Tron was exploited by a transaction rollback attack, allowing an attacker to drain 6,588 TRX (around $1,500,$2,000 at the time). The incident was executed just after the contract launched and emptied the contract balance, exploiting protocol logic weaknesses in how transaction state was handled.

LuckLambo104's contract failed to prevent or detect transaction rollback attacks on the Tron blockchain. This allowed an attacker contract to repeatedly manipulate game outcome transactions and profit by resetting or reversing their state, draining the DApp's balance soon after it launched.

name: Bitcoin Gold
label: 51% attack; Deep chain reorganization; Double-spend
rootCause:
Bitcoin Gold suffered a coordinated 51% attack in January 2020, resulting in double-spends totaling approximately $70,000. The attacker reorganized the chain twice, overruling exchange escrow periods and enabling fraudulent withdrawals.

Proof-of-work vulnerabilities allowed an attacker to rent or consolidate enough hashpower to exceed 51% of the Bitcoin Gold network, facilitating deep chain reorganizations and double-spend attacks against exchanges with insufficient confirmation requirements.

name: Fulcrum
label: Flash Loan
rootCause:
On January 11, 2020, Fulcrum released a flash loan feature on Ethereum Mainnet that exposed user funds to exploit risk through an atomic transaction vulnerability. The flaw enabled potential theft of $2.5 million from three pools. A white-hat intervention by 1inch demonstrated the risk before a malicious exploit occurred.

The vulnerability originated from the Fulcrum flash loan feature, which failed to account for atomic flash loan manipulation. The system made state-changing decisions on spot balances within a single transaction, allowing the possibility for an attacker to drain pool funds by exploiting flash loans without external price references or delay.

name: Nuls
label: Input Validation; Signature Verification Flaw
rootCause:
On December 23, 2019, the Nuls blockchain was exploited due to a reported signature verification flaw in version 2.2, enabling unauthorized transactions. Approximately 2 million NULS tokens (~$480,000) were stolen, with around 548,354 sold before detection. The network halted further loss by hard forking to destroy unrecoverable tokens.

A flaw in the transaction signature verification logic in Nuls version 2.2 allowed attackers to generate valid-looking transactions without legitimate authorization signatures. The technical specifics of the bypass remain undisclosed in public technical documentation.

name: VeChain
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
VeChain Foundation's buyback wallet was compromised through private key mishandling on 2019-12-14, resulting in the loss of around 1.1 billion VET tokens (~$6.5 million USD). The incident was traced to internal procedural failure. VeChain used governance controls to freeze a portion of stolen funds.

A finance team member created the buyback wallet outside of approved protocol, exposing its private key. This human error allowed unauthorized withdrawal of the wallet's entire balance.

name: Vertcoin
label: 51% attack; Double-spend
rootCause:
Vertcoin suffered a 51% proof-of-work reorganization on 2019-12-01 that reportedly replaced 603 blocks, invalidated five transactions, and redirected about 125 VTC worth roughly $29.

An attacker appears to have rented enough Lyra2REv3 hashpower to mine a heavier private fork, which Vertcoin's proof-of-work consensus accepted and which invalidated five earlier spends. The exact source of the hashpower remains unproven.

name: Upbit
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
On 2019-11-27, attackers transferred 342,000 ETH from an Upbit Ethereum hot wallet to an external address after gaining the ability to authorize withdrawals from the exchange's custody infrastructure. Upbit suspended deposits and withdrawals, moved remaining assets to cold storage, and stated that customer losses would be covered from corporate reserves.

Attackers obtained the ability to authorize transfers from Upbit's Ethereum hot wallet infrastructure. Public evidence supports a hot-wallet or signing-system compromise rather than a smart contract vulnerability. The exact intrusion path and method used to obtain signing authority have not been publicly disclosed.

name: VinDAX
label: Frontend Compromise; Key Leaked via Infrastructure
rootCause:
VinDAX, a Vietnam-based centralized cryptocurrency exchange, disclosed in November 2019 that attackers had withdrawn roughly $500,000 worth of assets across 23 cryptocurrencies. Public reporting confirms the losses and the exchange’s temporary suspension of deposits and withdrawals, but no detailed technical postmortem, attacker addresses, or verified on-chain theft transactions were published.

The exact intrusion path was never publicly disclosed. Contemporary reporting and later incident catalogues describe a compromise of exchange-controlled wallets or infrastructure credentials that enabled unauthorized withdrawals from VinDAX hot wallets.

name: Chain Fusion
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
Chain Fusion lost $6.4 million on Ethereum mainnet in September 2019 due to a private key compromise allowing attackers to drain protocol assets. All established facts originate from summary databases; technical details and on-chain evidence remain unavailable.

Attackers acquired a privileged protocol private key, granting sufficient authority to withdraw funds from the project’s contracts. The specific means of compromise, affected account, and implementation are unreported.

name: CoinTiger
label: Frontend Compromise; Key Leaked via Infrastructure
rootCause:
CoinTiger's cold wallet was breached, leading to the theft of 401,981,748 PTT tokens, with a reported loss of $9.2M. The theft was attributed to a leaked infrastructure key, affecting the Ethereum mainnet. Significant portions were frozen, but about 120M PTT entered the market.

A leak or compromise of the cold wallet's private key permitted unauthorized withdrawal of PTT tokens. The breach affected CoinTiger’s cold storage, which was expected to be segregated from online exposure. The mechanism was attributed to an infrastructure-related key exposure.

name: BitPoint
label: Hot wallet compromise; Unauthorized withdrawals
rootCause:
BITPoint disclosed a July 2019 hot-wallet breach after an XRP remittance anomaly exposed unauthorized withdrawals from BTC, BCH, ETH, LTC, and XRP custody. Public disclosures revised the loss to about ¥3.028 billion, but the entry path into the wallet environment was not established.

Unauthorized withdrawals were made from BITPoint's hot-wallet environment. The public record does not establish how the attacker obtained access to that environment or which control failed first.

name: Bitrue
label: Internal Process Vulnerability; Access Control
rootCause:
Attackers exploited a vulnerability in Bitrue exchange's internal risk review process on June 27, 2019, enabling unauthorized access to user funds. 9.3 million XRP and 2.5 million ADA were stolen, with a portion frozen and recovered. The incident resulted in net losses of approximately $3.15 million, and affected users' holdings were reimbursed by Bitrue.

Attackers exploited insufficient access controls in Bitrue's risk review process, allowing unauthorized transfers from user accounts and the exchange's hot wallet.

name: Synthetix v1+v2
label: Oracle Misconfiguration; Price Manipulation
rootCause:
Synthetix v1+v2 experienced an oracle misconfiguration on Ethereum Mainnet on June 25, 2019. An arbitrage bot exploited an inflated KRW price feed, converting sKRW to sETH for over 37 million synthetic Ether. The assets were returned after the team negotiated a bounty. No confirmed dollar-value loss was reported.

Synthetix's oracle aggregation failed to handle price-feed outages properly. When two of three KRW sources went offline, the system averaged only the remaining faulty feed, producing a 1000× inflated KRW/USD rate. There was no outlier rejection or anomaly detection, allowing the bot to exploit the mispricing repeatedly.

name: GateHub
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised; API Token Abuse
rootCause:
GateHub’s XRP wallet infrastructure was compromised in June 2019, resulting in losses of approximately 23.2 million XRP (about $9.5 million USD at the time) from more than 100 affected wallets. The breach was enabled by the attacker gaining access to valid wallet encryption tokens and exploiting GateHub’s API to access and drain user funds.

Attackers gained access to valid API tokens and exploited GateHub’s internal storage, enabling them to decrypt and access user XRP wallet private keys. This allowed them to initiate unauthorized transfers and drain funds from user accounts.

name: Kraken BTC/CAD flash crash
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
Kraken’s BTC/CAD market flash-crashed on 2019-06-02 after a suspected account compromise, with public reports tying the incident to about 1,200 BTC and roughly $10.45 million in reported loss.

The public record points to a compromised Kraken account and a very thin BTC/CAD order book that let an attacker convert customer BTC into fills on an attacker-controlled account at a sharply distorted price. The exact compromise path into the account, and any exchange-side reversal or recovery action, are not independently confirmed.

name: Poker EOS
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
Poker EOS lost over 26,900 EOS due to private key compromise on May 24, 2019. The attacker accessed multiple project accounts and withdrew funds to exchanges. The loss resulted from improper private key management, with no evidence of recovery.

The attacker obtained the project account's private key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals from Poker EOS accounts. The access was attributed to improper key management by the Poker EOS team.

name: Binance
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
On May 7, 2019, Binance’s Bitcoin hot wallet was compromised in a single large-scale withdrawal. Hackers obtained user API keys and 2FA codes via undisclosed methods, bypassed security checks, and stole about 7,000 BTC (≈$40.7 million). Binance covered user losses through its SAFU fund and suspended withdrawals for a security review.

Attackers compromised user API keys and 2FA codes, allowing unauthorized access to Binance’s Bitcoin hot wallet. Security checks failed to detect the aggregate withdrawal across multiple compromised accounts, enabling the mass theft.

name: TronBank
label: Rug Pull; Backdoor Contract
rootCause:
TronBank's Tron contract drained 26.73 million TRX in early May 2019 after a withdrawal path accepted an exact 0.011911 TRX value and released the full balance. Public records disagree on whether the theft happened on 2019-04-29 or 2019-05-03, but they agree on roughly $4.27 million lost.

A hidden withdrawal branch in the deployed TronBank contract released the entire balance when msg.value equaled 0x2E87, or 0.011911 TRX. The public record also says the verified TSC source did not match the mainnet logic, but it does not establish who introduced the mismatch.

name: TronBank
label: Token-ID bypass; Fake token deposit; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
On April 11, 2019, TronBank on the Tron blockchain was exploited when attackers used a fake BTTx token to bypass token ID checks and drain approximately 170 million genuine BTT tokens from the rewards pool. No exploit or recovery transactions have been independently verified.

The invest() function in the TronBank contract failed to enforce a tokenID check, allowing deposits of counterfeit tokens (BTTx) that triggered reward allocation and withdrawal of genuine BTT.

name: TronWow
label: Bet logic flaw; Frontend validation bypass
rootCause:
TronWow, a dice game DApp on Tron, was exploited on 11 April 2019 via a contract flaw in betting parameter validation. Attackers directly invoked the contract to place bets guaranteeing 100% win rates and much higher payouts than allowed, extracting 2.16 million TRX. No direct attack transactions or contract addresses are publicly available.

The TronWow contract failed to enforce server-side restrictions on bet parameters. By bypassing frontend limits, attackers supplied crafted inputs to the placeBet function that ensured every bet would win with inflated payout multipliers. The contract only checked win probability, not that the bet mask values matched game rules, enabling systematic extraction of funds.

name: Bithumb
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
On March 29, 2019, Bithumb's hot wallets for EOS and XRP were compromised by unauthorized access to private keys, resulting in the theft of approximately $19 million worth of cryptocurrency. Bithumb suspected insider involvement and responded by suspending withdrawals, moving remaining funds to cold storage, and initiating an internal investigation.

The incident was caused by hot wallet key compromise, allowing unauthorized withdrawals. Bithumb suspected insider action and single-key management of its EOS and XRP hot wallets, but there is no detailed technical disclosure. No evidence of external malware or phishing was found.

name: TronCrush
label: Logic Error; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
TronCrush on Tron was exploited on March 29, 2019, due to a transfer logic flaw that allowed attackers to mint over 150,000 TCC tokens without foundation by sending transfers to their own address. The specific economic impact is unknown, as no USD loss or withdrawal records have been reported.

The contract's transfer function did not check that the sender and recipient were different, allowing attackers to trigger transfers to themselves and mint new tokens without legitimate backing.

name: Coinbene
label: Access Control; Improper Access Control
rootCause:
CoinBene's Ethereum hot wallet experienced large, unauthorized outflows of ERC-20 tokens on March 25, 2019, totaling over $45 million as externally estimated. The event is generally attributed to suspected wallet compromise or failed access controls, but no technical root cause was disclosed. Loss figures reflect tokens moved, not confirmed unrecoverable loss.

Unauthorized wallet transfers consistent with hot-wallet key compromise or failed privileged access controls. No technical vulnerability, contract bug, or detailed method was disclosed by CoinBene.

name: DragonEx
label: Frontend Compromise; Key Leaked via Infrastructure
rootCause:
DragonEx lost about $7 million on 24 March 2019 after exchange signing material was exposed through an infrastructure compromise, allowing unauthorized withdrawals across multiple chains.

The public record supports compromise of DragonEx infrastructure that exposed private keys or equivalent signing authority for hot wallets. The exact initial access path remains unknown.

name: Etbox
label: Key Leaked via Infrastructure
rootCause:
Etbox’s wallet was hacked in March 2019, and the public record supports about $132,000 in losses across Bitcoin and Ethereum Mainnet. The exact leaked credential and transfer trace were not publicly documented.

The public record classifies the incident as a key leak via infrastructure and a wallet hack, but it does not identify the exact leaked credential, the exposed host, or the transfer path.

name: Coinbin
label: Admin Drain; Rug Pull
rootCause:
Coinbin, a South Korean cryptocurrency exchange, suffered an internal theft of private keys by a senior employee in February 2019, resulting in a loss of approximately $26 million and bankruptcy. The incident was not a smart contract exploit, but an administrative drain due to insufficient controls over wallet access.

A senior Coinbin employee, formerly the CEO of Youbit, appropriated private keys for multiple cryptocurrency wallets,intentionally losing keys and embezzling assets. The lack of separation between critical administrative duties and unrestricted access enabled the theft, resulting in bankruptcy.

name: LocalBitcoins
label: Forum-based phishing attack; Credential and 2FA theft via third-party software compromise
rootCause:
LocalBitcoins suffered a security breach on January 26, 2019, after attackers used a forum-based phishing scheme to steal 7.95 BTC (about $27,000) from at least six user accounts. The exploit stemmed from a vulnerability in third-party forum software, allowing redirection to a fraudulent login page that captured credentials and two-factor codes.

Attackers exploited a vulnerability in LocalBitcoins' third-party forum software, redirecting users to a phishing site that captured login and 2FA credentials, enabling unauthorized withdrawals from user accounts.

name: Cryptopia
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
On January 14, 2019, Cryptopia suffered a major key compromise that allowed attackers to systematically drain an estimated $16 million in ETH and ERC-20 tokens from over 76,000 per-user deposit addresses. The attackers obtained access to the exchange's hot-wallet infrastructure, leading to prolonged multi-day losses and eventual bankruptcy.

Compromise of the private keys governing Cryptopia’s hot-wallet infrastructure enabled unauthorized access and transfer of assets. Since customers’ balances were held in thousands of per-user derived wallets, the compromise granted control over all these addresses.

name: Ethereum Classic
label: 51% attack; double spend; deep chain reorganization
rootCause:
Ethereum Classic suffered a January 2019 51% reorganization that enabled repeated double-spends on the proof-of-work chain. Public reporting placed the affected amount at 219,500 ETC.

Ethereum Classic's proof-of-work consensus allowed an attacker with majority hashpower to mine a private fork, publish the heavier branch, and replace previously credited history. That let the attacker double-spend exchange deposits during the reorganization window.

name: ToBet
label: Node sync/replay exploit; Protocol Logic flaw
rootCause:
ToBet, an EOS gambling dApp, was exploited on 18,19 December 2018. Reports attribute a loss of about 22,000 EOS to an attacker exploiting node synchronization flaws, although no primary code or on-chain transaction evidence is available.

ToBet was vulnerable to node sync and replay exploitation: the attacker selectively submitted only winning bets by exploiting differences in API and BP node confirmation, allowing profit without contract-level vulnerabilities.

name: EOS Max
label: Protocol Logic; Consensus / node synchronization issue
rootCause:
EOS Max, an EOS gambling dapp, was reportedly exploited on 2018-12-18 through an EOS node synchronization and speculative execution issue that let attackers selectively submit winning bets. Public reporting attributed roughly 55,526 EOS in losses to EOS Max, but no primary transaction record or official postmortem was located.

Available reporting attributed the EOS Max incident to EOS node synchronization and speculative execution behavior between API nodes and block producer nodes. Attackers reportedly executed bets against locally observed outcomes and only finalized favorable transactions on block producer nodes before block irreversibility. No verified EOS Max contract vulnerability, historical contract source, or primary incident disclosure was located in the available evidence.

name: Vertcoin
label: 51% Attack; Chain Reorganization; Double Spend
rootCause:
Vertcoin suffered a series of 51% attacks between October and December 2018, resulting in repeated chain reorganizations and reported double-spending losses estimated at $100,000. The attacker rented large amounts of hashpower to overpower the Vertcoin network, enabling deep reorganizations and successful double-spend transactions mainly targeting exchanges.

The root cause was Vertcoin's vulnerability to 51% attacks due to insufficient mining decentralization. The attacker rented hashpower via cloud mining services, gained control of the chain, and orchestrated deep reorgs to double-spend deposited coins.

name: EOS Lelego
label: Random number logic flaw; Predictable contract state variables
rootCause:
On 19 November 2018, the EOS Lelego betting game was exploited via a random number vulnerability, allowing the attacker to win an abnormal rate of games and withdraw a reported 6,500 EOS. The contract operations were rapidly suspended to prevent further losses. The technical exploitation method is broadly inferred from contemporaneous EOS quiz game attacks, but no public Lelego code or transaction hashes are available.

EOS Lelego used a random number generation mechanism with attacker-influenced or predictable contract variables, enabling outcome prediction and repeated winning. This logic flaw created an abnormal win rate, but the specific implementation exploited remains unconfirmed due to the absence of public source code.

name: AurumCoin
label: 51% attack; double-spend
rootCause:
AurumCoin suffered a November 2018 51% attack that let an attacker reverse a Cryptopia withdrawal and double-spend 15,752.26 AU, reported at about $500,000 at the time.

AurumCoin’s low-hashrate SHA-256 chain was vulnerable to majority-hashrate reorganization, which allowed a double-spend against Cryptopia’s wallet. No vulnerable contract code applies; the failure was at the consensus and exchange-finality boundary.

name: HireVibes AirDropsDAC
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
The HireVibes AirDropsDAC EOS airdrop service was exploited on November 12, 2018, when a developer test account’s private key was inadvertently published to a public Github repository. Attackers used the compromised key to siphon HVT and ZKS tokens, selling at least 2,514 EOS (~$13,600) via Newdex and consolidating proceeds in attacker addresses.

A developer's test account private key was publicly exposed on Github as part of a testnet script repository. The attacker obtained the compromised key and used it to transfer airdrop tokens from AirDropsDAC, liquidate them, and move the proceeds off-platform.

name: EOS.WIN
label: Random number manipulation; Contract logic error
rootCause:
EOS.WIN, an EOS gambling DApp, was exploited on November 11,12, 2018, allowing attackers to manipulate the random number generation process and gain profits of roughly 9,180 EOS. The attack used multiple coordinated accounts to predict lottery outcomes, exploiting game state and inline transaction rollback.

The random number generator used in the EOS.WIN game contract included attacker-controllable variables, specifically the bet_id (lottery serial number), which allowed coordinated accounts to manipulate the outcome by sending simultaneous transactions and predicting the generated random number. Inline call failure and state rollback further enabled attackers to optimize their chances.

name: EOSDice
label: Pseudo-random number vulnerability
rootCause:
EOSDice, a gambling dApp on the EOS blockchain, was exploited twice in November 2018 due to predictable pseudo-random number generation. Attackers manipulated refer block data and contract balances to predetermine game outcomes, extracting an estimated $25,100 in EOS. No on-chain transaction or contract source for the exploit is publicly verified.

EOSDice's random number function relied on blockchain values and contract balances that were controllable or predictable by attackers. Deferred execution and EOS notification order allowed adversaries to coordinate betting, notification, and balance manipulation so random outcomes could be calculated or guaranteed before placing bets.

name: FFGame
label: Logic Error
rootCause:
FFGame, an EOS-based gaming dApp, was exploited on November 8, 2018, due to its use of predictable random number generation. The attacker repeatedly won by precomputing outcomes, resulting in the loss of approximately 1,331 EOS (roughly $7,200 at the time). Funds were transferred to the Huobi exchange, with no public evidence of recovery or patch from developers.

FFGame's smart contract relied on deterministic on-chain data for randomness. This made its random number generation predictable, allowing an attacker to precompute game outcomes and place winning bets with high accuracy.

name: Gate.io
label: Frontend Compromise; Supply Chain Attack
rootCause:
On November 7, 2018, Gate.io was compromised through a supply-chain attack on its third-party analytics provider StatCounter. Malicious code injected into StatCounter's JavaScript targeted Gate.io's Bitcoin withdrawal page, replacing user-specified addresses with attacker-controlled Bitcoin addresses. The extent of user loss remains unknown, as the attack generated new recipient addresses for each withdrawal and no public on-chain transactions have been confirmed.

Attackers injected malicious JavaScript into StatCounter's analytics script, which Gate.io loaded on its withdrawal page. The code checked for the withdrawal URI, loaded a second-stage script from a lookalike domain, and replaced user-entered Bitcoin addresses with attacker-controlled ones. Gate.io's lack of strict supply-chain validation for such critical scripts enabled the attack.

name: EOSCast
label: Logic Error; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
EOSCast was exploited on EOS on 31 October 2018, resulting in a loss of approximately $73,000. The exploit was enabled by a contract logic flaw that allowed unbacked token minting through improper transfer validation in the contract’s apply handler.

The EOSCast contract failed to validate the sender of transfer actions within its apply method, allowing attackers to mint tokens without a corresponding deposit. This is an infinite mint vulnerability caused by missing transfer source checks.

name: EosRoyale
label: Predictable Randomness
rootCause:
EosRoyale, an EOS gambling application, was exploited on 2018-10-26 through predictable on-chain randomness. Contemporary EOS security reporting stated that attackers calculated future game outcomes from previous block information, leading to reported losses of about 10,800 EOS. Later incident catalogues estimated the impact near $60,000.

EosRoyale reportedly derived game randomness from deterministic EOS chain data that attackers could reproduce off-chain. Contemporary incident reporting stated that attackers calculated future random numbers from previous block information. The vulnerable historical contract source and exact random number implementation were not recovered.

name: EOSBet
label: Donation Attack; Logic Error
rootCause:
On October 15, 2018, attackers exploited a smart contract vulnerability in the EOSBet gambling application on EOS, using a donation attack to siphon approximately $338,000 in EOS from the platform. The exploit allowed malicious users to trigger unauthorized fund transfers from EOSBet’s operational accounts to attacker-controlled wallets.

EOSBet’s smart contract trusted the origin of incoming EOS transfers and allowed unverified transfer logic. Attackers injected malicious code into their accounts, sending specifically crafted EOS token transfers that caused the contract to match their deposit with an equal outgoing transfer from the platform’s operational wallet. The contract failed to distinguish between genuine game deposits and attacker-triggered, fraudulent actions, resulting in a loss of funds.

name: SpankChain
label: Reentrancy
rootCause:
SpankChain's payment channel contract on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited on 7 October 2018 via a reentrancy vulnerability. The attacker used a malicious token contract to repeatedly withdraw funds, draining 165 ETH (~$38,000 at the time). All stolen funds, including ETH and BOOTY tokens, were later recovered after the attacker provided the private key to SpankChain.

The LedgerChannel contract violated the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern by calling an external token's transfer function before deleting channel state within the LCOpenTimeout() function. This allowed a malicious token contract to re-enter LCOpenTimeout and repeatedly withdraw funds from the same channel before its state was deleted.

name: NewDex
label: Infinite Mint
rootCause:
On September 14, 2018, NewDex's EOS-based exchange was exploited when attackers minted fake 'EOS' tokens and exchanged them for genuine assets. The backend treated deposits based on token names alone, resulting in losses estimated at $58,000. No primary chain or code evidence confirms asset flow or compensation.

NewDex relied on token names rather than contract origin for deposits. The attacker exploited EOS’s permissionless token creation to mint counterfeit 'EOS' tokens, which NewDex accepted as legitimate collateral. No contract address validation was enforced.

name: Zaif
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Credential Compromise
rootCause:
Zaif, a Japanese cryptocurrency exchange, suffered a hot wallet key compromise on September 14, 2018, resulting in the theft of approximately $60 million in BTC, Bitcoin Cash, and MonaCoin. The attackers exploited poor wallet security to access and drain assets.

Unauthorized access to Zaif’s hot wallet was enabled by compromised credentials, allowing attackers to obtain the private key or API access and execute large fund withdrawals. Lack of real-time monitoring or robust anomaly detection allowed the theft to proceed unnoticed.

name: EOSBet
label: Logic error; Unchecked transfer function; Infinite mint
rootCause:
On 12 September 2018, EOSBet on EOS was exploited through a smart contract bug that allowed unauthorized withdrawals, resulting in an estimated loss of $200,000 (about 40,000 EOS). The contract failed to enforce input validation and assertion checks, enabling attackers to mint or extract tokens beyond legitimate deposits.

A flawed transfer function in EOSBet’s contract allowed external calls without proper input validation or assertion checks, enabling attackers to bypass authorization and illegitimately mint or withdraw tokens. This led to an 'infinite mint' vulnerability.

name: KICKICO
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
KICKICO suffered a major key compromise on Ethereum on 26 July 2018. Attackers used the stolen private key to destroy tokens at user addresses and recreate them at attacker-controlled addresses, affecting approximately 70 million KICK tokens valued around $7.7 million. The operator replaced the compromised key and committed to restoring user balances. No primary on-chain evidence or verified remediation record has been found.

The single private key controlling the KICKICO token contract was compromised. This allowed attackers to burn tokens at legitimate user addresses and mint them in attacker-controlled wallets, with no secondary validation or multisig safeguard in place.

name: Bancor V3
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
On July 9, 2018, Bancor's Ethereum deployment suffered a hot wallet key compromise, resulting in losses of approximately $23.5 million across ETH, BNT, and NPXS. The attackers accessed a wallet responsible for contract upgrades, withdrew tokens, and forced Bancor to freeze its own BNT while collaborating with exchanges in unsuccessful attempts to block the liquidation of ETH and NPXS.

An attacker obtained the private key for Bancor's upgrade wallet, allowing unauthorized withdrawals of token balances controlled by Bancor's contracts.

name: Bithumb
label: Key Leaked via Infrastructure; Hot Wallet Compromise
rootCause:
On June 20,21, 2018, Bithumb, a major South Korean cryptocurrency exchange, lost approximately $31 million from its hot wallets during a breach of its exchange infrastructure. The attack did not involve a smart contract or frontend exploit; instead, hot wallet key compromise enabled unauthorized withdrawals. Subsequent efforts recovered about 45 percent of funds, with the exact method of initial intrusion and all affected addresses undisclosed.

Attackers obtained unauthorized access to the private keys for Bithumb's hot wallets via an exchange infrastructure compromise. No technical postmortem or public forensic report confirms the specific method of that intrusion.

name: Coinrail
label: Unauthorized access to exchange wallet; Operational security failure
rootCause:
Coinrail, a South Korean cryptocurrency exchange, was hacked on June 10, 2018, resulting in an estimated $40 million loss in ERC-20 tokens. Attackers accessed hot wallets managed by the exchange, prompting freezing measures by token issuers and urgent asset shifts by Coinrail.

Attackers compromised Coinrail's operational wallet infrastructure, gaining unauthorized access to hot wallets. Public evidence points to an off-chain security failure rather than a smart contract bug.

name: ZenCash
label: 51% attack; Double-spend; Hashpower rental
rootCause:
On June 2, 2018, the ZenCash blockchain suffered a 51% attack, enabling the attacker to double-spend approximately 23,000 ZEN (around $550,000) by reorganizing 38 blocks. The attacker used rented or concentrated Equihash hashpower to privately mine a longer chain, targeting exchanges with inadequate confirmation requirements. The incident exposed fundamental vulnerabilities of small proof-of-work networks to hashpower manipulation.

The Equihash-based ZenCash blockchain was vulnerable to 51% attacks because an attacker could cheaply acquire enough hashpower,via rented mining resources or private mining,to control block production, enabling deep chain reorganizations and double-spend attacks against exchanges with insufficient deposit confirmation delays.

name: Verge
label: Consensus Manipulation; Timestamp Spoofing; Double Spend
rootCause:
On May 22, 2018, Verge (XVG) suffered a major consensus exploit that enabled attackers to mine fraudulent blocks using timestamp spoofing and algorithm abuse, resulting in the theft of approximately $1.7 million worth of XVG.

The incident was caused by a consensus vulnerability in Verge's multi-algorithm proof-of-work protocol. Attackers spoofed block timestamps to repeatedly mine blocks with the same algorithm, bypassing intended mining restrictions and enabling malicious chain reorganization and double-spending.

name: Bitcoin Gold
label: 51% Attack; Double-Spend; Chain Reorganization
rootCause:
Bitcoin Gold suffered a coordinated 51% attack in May 2018, enabling the attacker to double-spend over 388,000 BTG ($18 million) at exchanges by manipulating the chain and withdrawing funds from fraudulent deposits before detection.

The root cause was a low total network hashrate combined with the Equihash (Zhash) mining algorithm, which allowed the attacker to rent or coordinate enough hashpower to consistently control more than 50% of the Bitcoin Gold network. This enabled deep chain reorganizations and double-spend attacks targeting exchanges.

name: Monacoin
label: 51% attack; Double-spend; Block withholding
rootCause:
Between May 13 and 15, 2018, Monacoin suffered a 51% attack that allowed a malicious mining pool to double-spend coins by manipulating block confirmations. Approximately $90,000 in MONA was withdrawn from exchanges before detection. The attack exploited a weakness in Monacoin’s difficulty retargeting algorithm, but no protocol or code patch was immediately deployed.

A flaw in Monacoin's mining difficulty retargeting logic enabled a mining pool with majority hashrate to rapidly mine and withhold blocks, privately extending the chain and enabling double-spend attacks against exchanges.

name: SmartMesh
label: Integer Overflow; Unchecked Arithmetic; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
On April 24, 2018, SmartMesh's ERC-20 token contract on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited via an unchecked integer overflow in its transferProxy function. The vulnerability enabled attackers to generate vast amounts of counterfeit tokens. Nearly all fake SMT were frozen and destroyed by exchanges, limiting the impact to a small fraction traded before response.

Unchecked arithmetic in the transferProxy function allowed integer overflow when summing value and fee parameters, enabling minting of arbitrarily large token amounts outside intended supply controls.

name: BeautyChain
label: Integer Overflow; Infinite Mint
rootCause:
A critical integer overflow bug in BeautyChain’s BEC token contract on Ethereum allowed attackers to mint an arbitrary number of tokens on 22 April 2018 using batchTransfer, causing catastrophic supply inflation and trading suspensions. No fully verified recovery or precise loss figure is available.

The BEC token’s batchTransfer function multiplied the number of recipients by the sent value without proper overflow protection, allowing attackers to overflow the internal computation and bypass balance checks, minting tokens far beyond their real holdings.

name: Gate.io
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
On April 21, 2018, Gate.io suffered a large-scale theft attributed to private key compromise, resulting in losses estimated at $235 million. Official technical details, affected wallet lists, and recovery status remain undisclosed; all established loss figures and chain activity come from secondary investigator reports.

Gate.io’s operational wallet private keys were compromised, enabling the attacker to conduct direct mass withdrawals. The specific method of compromise (phishing, insider, infrastructure attack, or key management flaw) is not publicly documented.

name: Coinsecure
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
Coinsecure, a major Indian cryptocurrency exchange, lost 438 Bitcoin (~$3.3M) in April 2018 when its primary wallet's private key was compromised during a Bitcoin Gold extraction operation. Legal accusations and internal disputes followed, but there is no evidence of funds recovery or detailed technical disclosure.

The primary wallet's private key was exposed or misused during an internal extraction process, allowing an unauthorized transfer of Bitcoin out of Coinsecure's control. The precise mechanism is unverified, but evidence points to improper key management or potential insider misuse.

name: BitGrail
label: Withdrawal logic idempotency failure; Exchange access control failure
rootCause:
BitGrail, an Italian cryptocurrency exchange, lost approximately 17 million Nano (XRB) valued around $170 million in a prolonged multi-stage exploit culminating in February 2018. Attackers abused a withdrawal system flaw that permitted multiple Nano withdrawals on the same balance, draining the exchange's hot wallet.

BitGrail's withdrawal system failed to implement idempotency and double-spend prevention, allowing attackers to submit repeated withdrawal requests for the same Nano deposit. The system credited and executed these withdrawals multiple times, draining funds beyond customer balances.

name: Coincheck
label: Malware via phishing; Hot wallet single-key compromise; Lack of multisig; No cold storage segregation
rootCause:
On 26 January 2018, Coincheck's NEM (XEM) hot wallet was compromised, leading to the theft of approximately 523 million XEM (then worth ~$530 million). The attacker gained access through malware installed via a targeted phishing campaign against engineering staff, exploiting the absence of multisig and cold storage. The stolen funds were laundered quickly, resulting in minimal on-chain recovery. Coincheck reimbursed customers from corporate funds and was later acquired by Monex Group.

Coincheck stored its entire NEM holding in a single hot wallet secured by a single private key, without multisig or cold-storage segregation. The operational failure allowed malware delivered via spear-phishing to steal the key, enabling an attacker to authorize the massive withdrawal.

name: EtherDelta
label: DNS Hijack; Frontend Phishing
rootCause:
EtherDelta's DNS records were compromised in December 2017. Attackers redirected users to a phishing frontend, obtaining their keys and stealing both ETH and tokens. Estimated losses reached $1.4 million, but no contract bug was involved.

The root cause was a DNS hijacking of EtherDelta's website, allowing attackers to serve a fraudulent frontend to users and capture their wallet credentials.

name: Youbit
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
On 19 December 2017, Youbit, a South Korean cryptocurrency exchange, suffered a major compromise of its hot wallet on Bitcoin, resulting in the loss of approximately 17% of its total assets. The incident forced the exchange to shut down operations and file for bankruptcy. The exact loss amount remains undisclosed.

Attackers gained access to the private keys of Youbit's hot wallet, allowing them to withdraw a significant portion of the exchange's funds.

name: NiceHash
label: Frontend Compromise; Key Leaked via Infrastructure
rootCause:
NiceHash lost about 4,736 BTC, roughly $64 million at the time, after attackers used compromised employee credentials to drain the company’s Bitcoin wallet infrastructure in December 2017.

Compromised employee credentials gave the attacker access to NiceHash’s payment and wallet systems. Public reporting points to phishing or a compromised company workstation as the initial foothold, but the exact entry path was never published in a technical postmortem.

name: Tether
label: Key Compromise; Private Key Compromised
rootCause:
On November 19, 2017, Tether's treasury wallet on the Bitcoin blockchain was compromised, resulting in the unauthorized transfer of approximately $30.95 million USDT to an external address. Tether issued a protocol-level freeze to prevent these tokens from entering circulation.

The root cause was a breach of Tether's treasury wallet, which was apparently protected by a single private key. The attacker gained access to this key and executed an unauthorized USDT transfer via Omni Layer, exposing the risk of single-key wallet custody.

name: Parity Multisig
label: Access Control; Uninitialized Delegatecall Library; Selfdestruct Exposure
rootCause:
In November 2017, a critical bug in Parity's multisig wallet design allowed an external user to gain ownership of a shared library contract and self-destruct it. This destroyed essential logic for all dependent wallets, permanently freezing over 513,000 ETH on Ethereum mainnet.

The shared WalletLibrary contract was deployed without restricting direct initialization. Any external caller could invoke its public initWallet function to claim ownership and call kill, executing selfdestruct. Proxy-based multisigs relying on this library lost access when the code was erased.

name: CoinDash
label: Frontend Compromise
rootCause:
The CoinDash ICO suffered a frontend website compromise during launch on July 17, 2017, with investors sending over $7 million worth of ETH to a fraudulent address after the attacker replaced the official wallet. CoinDash halted the sale, investigated, and committed to issuing tokens to affected contributors who sent ETH before the shutdown.

A website frontend compromise allowed an attacker to modify the public ETH contribution address displayed to investors during the ICO. No cryptographic attestation or verification mechanism was in place to assure address authenticity.

name: Parity
label: Access Control; Uninitialized Proxy
rootCause:
The Parity multisig wallet vulnerability on Ethereum Mainnet in July 2017 allowed an attacker to take ownership of high-profile wallets by calling an unprotected initialization function. The attacker drained over 153,000 ETH (~$30M at the time) from three major crowdsale wallets. A white-hat group later rescued additional funds using the same exploit.

The Parity multisig proxy architecture exposed an unprotected initializer function via delegatecall, allowing anyone to reinitialize ownership after deployment and drain funds. No access control or one-time-use guard was enforced.

name: Yapizon
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
Yapizon, a South Korean Bitcoin exchange, was breached on April 22, 2017 when attackers gained access to the private keys for four hot wallets, resulting in a theft of about 3,816 BTC (≈$4.8M at the time). The loss forced the exchange to reduce all user balances by 37% and issue IOU tokens, with no funds ever recovered.

Attackers compromised the private keys to Yapizon's operational hot wallets, enabling unauthorized withdrawal of all assets held in those wallets.

name: Bitcurex
label: Key Compromise; Hot Wallet Key Compromised
rootCause:
Bitcurex, a major Polish Bitcoin exchange, suffered a critical security breach in October 2016. Roughly 2,300 BTC (~$1.5 million) were stolen from exchange-managed hot wallets, forcing a shutdown and leading to user asset loss with no clear evidence of recovery.

Bitcurex lost control of hot wallet private keys following an external breach, allowing unauthorized withdrawal of exchange-held customer funds. No evidence establishes a specific technical vulnerability or insider involvement.

name: Bitfinex
label: Multisignature key compromise (secondary reporting from Ledger Labs summary); Operational security/practice (co-storage of keys); Hot wallet/online device compromise
rootCause:
On August 2, 2016, Bitfinex suffered a security breach on Bitcoin resulting in the theft of 119,755 BTC (roughly $72 million at the time). Attackers exploited a flaw in multisignature wallet key management, but exact technical details remain based on secondary sources, as the full post-incident report and code are not public.

Attackers were able to access enough multisignature wallet keys to initiate mass unauthorized withdrawals. Secondary reporting indicates this was likely due to a key management flaw that stored two required signing keys on the same system, bypassing intended multi-party controls. This technical mechanism is not officially confirmed by Bitfinex or BitGo.

name: The DAO
label: Reentrancy
rootCause:
On June 17, 2016, The DAO contract on Ethereum Mainnet was exploited via a reentrancy bug in its splitDAO function, allowing an attacker to recursively withdraw funds and drain approximately 3.6 million ETH (worth about $60 million at the time) into a child DAO.
